Trump says war will end and gas prices to fall after the midterms
President Donald Trump said the war will end and gas prices will come down after the midterms.
"I think the war is going to end immediately after the election. I think the war will end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," he told reporters on Wednesday.
Iran condemns IAEA resolution on its nuclear program

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi condemned the International Atomic Energy Agency's resolution on the country's nuclear program on Wednesday, saying that the resolution is based on "fabrications" and will not achieve what its signatories intend.

"They attack Iran's nuclear facilities under safeguards, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to issue a resolution at the Board of Governors," Gharibabadi wrote in a post on X.

The IAEA reported Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at various undeclared sites in Iran, according to the Associated Press.
The resolution was put forward by the U.S., Britain, France and Germany, according to the AP.
Tanker hit by projectile off Iraqi coast, vessel listing off UAE, UKMTO says
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre said that it received a report of a tanker being attacked in the northern Persian Gulf on Wednesday morning.
The tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile" south-east of Al-Faw, Iraq, the UKMTO alert said. "Crew are reported safe and there is no environmental impact reported at this time," the UKMTO added.

Also on Wednesday, the UKMTO issued another report of a vessel spotted listing off Port Rashid in the United Arab Emirates, "possibly indicating water ingress following an attack from an unknown projectile."
Iran says attacks on Jordan, US Navy vessels were 'defensive'
Iran on Wednesday condemned the latest U.S. attacks on Iranian oil tankers and said its subsequent strikes on regional U.S. targets were in self-defense.

"The aggressive actions by the United States against Iranian commercial vessels not only represent a dangerous escalation of tensions in the region but also constitute an outright threat to regional and international peace and security," the Iranian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

The ministry said its subsequent "defensive strikes" targeted "U.S. military bases and facilities located in Jordan that continue to support U.S. military aggressions against Iran, as well as several U.S. aggressive vessels."
Iranian forces, it added, "will not hesitate to exercise their inherent right of self-defense and will respond decisively and appropriately to any enemy military aggression."
-ABC News' Morgan Winsor

title: Live updates: Republicans kick off first-ever midterm convention
summary: President Trump is giving a keynote address on Wednesday evening.
story: President Trump will give the keynote address Wednesday evening.

President Donald Trump and Republicans from across the country are in Dallas, Texas, for two nights to support the slate of candidates running this year and to tout the administration's agenda going into November in their first-ever midterm convention.
Trump will deliver the first session's keynote address on Wednesday evening.
Key Headlines

4 minutes agoTexas trucker who voted for Trump says Iran war, diesel prices pushing him to Dems1 hour and 1 minute agoImages of Trump line the walls2 hours and 47 minutes agoTrump says some Republicans not coming to convention because ‘we don’t have room’
4 minutes agoTexas trucker who voted for Trump says Iran war, diesel prices pushing him to Dems
1 hour and 1 minute agoImages of Trump line the walls
2 hours and 47 minutes agoTrump says some Republicans not coming to convention because ‘we don’t have room’
Texas trucker who voted for Trump says Iran war, diesel prices pushing him to Dems

GRAPEVINE, Texas -- Down the road from the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Mike Njenga's trucking company is struggling. His diesel fuel expenses have skyrocketed because of the Iran war -- forcing him to take trucks off the road and pass price hikes to customers.
Njenga voted for Trump and has been happy to back Republicans for years. But he told ABC News' Rachel Scott he is strongly considering voting for Democrat James Talarico for Senate in November.

"Whether he's conservative, whether you're liberal, at this point, all I care [about] is economics," he said. "I want to make sure things I can survive in business. I want to make sure I'm going to be able to feed my kids."
Njenga's situation underscores the challenge Republicans face as they try to excite their base heading into the fall, and how Trump's handling of the economy and Iran war loom over all other issues.

Asked how he thinks Trump is handling the economy, Njenga replied, "Just looking at what is going on right now in the world and between the tariffs and the war in Iran, it's not very encouraging. I am disappointed."
-ABC News' Benjamin Siegel
Images of Trump line the walls
People have dubbed the midterm convention the "Trumpapalooza" as the president is expected to be at the center of the celebration.
So far, it looks like it -- photos of Trump line the walls at the American Airlines Center.
-ABC News' Hannah Demissie
Trump says some Republicans not coming to convention because ‘we don’t have room’
Trump said he anticipates a "tremendous crowd" at the convention but said some Republicans aren't coming due to a lack of space.

"I think we're going to have a tremendous crowd tonight. Sold out. Looks very big. Looks very exciting, and we're going to explain what we've done," Trump said as he was departing Joint Base Andrews for Dallas.
Asked by ABC's Mary Bruce about Republicans in key races who decided not to attend the convention, Trump said that "everybody is coming."
Trump argued that some people were not coming because there wasn't space, saying "we don't have room for 500 politicians."

"We have room for the ones that have a close race if they're slightly behind or slightly ahead or tied, but we don't have rooms for people that are 35 points up and don't need to be there," Trump said.
American Airlines Center in Dallas, where the convention is being held, can hold up to 20,000 people, according to American Airlines.
-ABC News' Isabella Murray and Nicholas Kerr
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker calls GOP convention a distraction

On the first day of the Republican's Midterm Convention, billionaire Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who is widely seen as a potential 2028 contender, held a press conference with Texas Democrats, where he argued this week’s events at the convention are serving as a distraction from the kitchen-table problems Americans are enduring.

"Donald Trump is hoping that a flashy primetime event will make you forget that well, his trade war is killing costs for families at the grocery store, his war in Iran is killing ranchers and farmers and their way of life,” Pritzker said.

As Democrats work to build a contrast to the Republican agenda throughout the Trump administration, Pritzker highlighted the unprecedented mid-century redistricting fight Texas Democrats endured last year, when many left the state to prevent a vote on new congressional maps in the state.

"In this moment, when America needs a new generation of leaders, fighters willing to stand up against tyranny, Texas Democrats have stepped into the breach. They alerted the nation to these dangers, and Texas Democrats set an example for the rest of America," he said.

Pritzker, who is running for reelection, punted when asked about his 2028 ambitions, but said, "anybody that is showing up here and bootlicking Donald Trump, and that's what this is all about, is probably going to be disqualified in 2028." Pritzker has not ruled out a presidential bid in 2028.
-ABC News' Juhi Doshi and Lalee Ibssa

title: Dangerous heat, humidity invades the West: Latest
summary: More than 90 million people from California to Kentucky are under alerts for dangerously hot conditions.
story: The temp will feel like 113 degrees on Wednesday in LA.
More than 90 million people from California to Kentucky are under alerts for dangerously hot conditions.
Southern California is experiencing temperatures 20 degrees above average and very rare humidity, with some local meteorologists calling this some of the most extreme conditions they can remember.
On Wednesday, the heat index -- what temperature it feels like with humidity -- is forecast to hit 113 degrees in Los Angeles, 102 degrees in San Diego, and 116 in Indio, California.
Extreme heat warnings are in place from San Diego to Las Vegas to Phoenix while a heat advisory is in place across California, from Bakersfield to San Francisco to Sacramento.
Cooler air will move in for Northern California and Southern California by Saturday, with the temperature forecast to drop to 85 degrees in Sacramento and 89 degrees in Burbank.

This extreme heat is also expanding east to the middle of the country. On Wednesday, the heat index is forecast to soar to 106 degrees in Dallas and Little Rock, Arkansas; 105 degrees in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma; 104 in Memphis, Tennessee; and 102 in Louisville, Kentucky.
Thursday may bring a break in the heat for some cities like Oklahoma City, but the high heat and humidity are likely to return Friday through Sunday.

title: Trump claims firefighters carried him from ground zero after 9/11 attack
summary: The White House shared no proof the incident occurred.
story: The White House shared no proof the incident occurred.

President Donald Trump, at an event earlier this week honoring those who died in the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attack, claimed that firefighters carried him away from ground zero when he visited the site in the days after the 9/11 attacks. It’s part of an evolution of the president's claims about his involvement in events in the days and weeks following the attack.

"I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened," Trump said during Tuesday’s Tunnel to Towers Foundation's event, repeating one of his claims that he brought hundreds of construction workers to ground zero after the 9/11 attack.

"The United States Steel building was creaking, really creaking, and we thought it was going to fall down," Trump said of what appeared to be a wobbly building, now known as One Liberty Plaza, nearby.

"We thought it was coming down on top of us, and two firemen, big, strong guys. And I'm not the smallest guy in the world. They grabbed me under the arms, said, 'Got to get out of here.' And they literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do. I’m big. They lifted me up and they started running with me,” Trump continued.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump was "relaying his experience of a city reeling" in the aftermath of the attacks, but shared no proof the incident occurred. Ingle pointed to online posts from the president on Tuesday night of images of him in New York City in the days after the attacks.
Trump's posts were prompted after New York Magazine called his story about the firefighters a "weird lie about where he was on 9/11."

"I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers,” Trump posted on social media on Tuesday, adding of his speech earlier in the day, "everything I said was exactly accurate."
It is not the first time Trump has told a version of this story, though there is no evidence it happened.

"I've never seen anything like I saw, and they heard a screech, and everybody thought that the U.S. Steel building was coming down and it was not so far from us," Trump said at a campaign event in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in January 2016. "And these two guys there were massive guys, two really big -- because I'm a big guy and they grabbed me. I must tell you, honestly, I never knew I could run that fast."
Over the years, Trump has made several other unsubstantiated claims about 9/11. One of those was that he saw the attack firsthand, though Trump Tower is four miles away from the site.

"I was looking out from a building in midtown Manhattan directly at the World Trade Center when I saw a second plane, at a tremendous speed, go into the second tower," Trump said at an anniversary event in 2019.
He also claimed to witness thousands of Muslim celebrating the attack.

"Hey, I watched when the World Trade Center came tumbling down. And I watched in Jersey City, New Jersey, where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down," Trump told rally goers in Birmingham, Alabama, in 2015. "Thousands of people were cheering."
It has never been confirmed that those massive celebrations happened, and Trump's campaign at the time failed to provide proof.

title: 9/11 air records released after years of fights against City Hall
summary: First responders who rushed to the World Trade Center on and immediately after the 9/11 attacks were likely exposed to dangerous toxins, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
story: "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied," the mayor said.

For nearly a quarter century, New Yorkers, Ground Zero workers, advocates and elected officials have called on City Hall to reveal the truth about what it knew about the air quality in downtown Manhattan after the 9/11 attacks.

On Tuesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani released tens of thousands of long-guarded city documents related to the air quality that showed how first responders who rushed to the World Trade Center were likely exposed to dangerous toxins.

The mayor's office released the first 170,000 pages of records via an online portal. It includes memos from city leaders and agencies going as far back as the Giuliani administration, which ran from 1994 to 2001.
Mamdani, who was joined by 9/11 responders and advocates at City Hall, said that New Yorkers needed to know the truth.
"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," he said.

"9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept. 11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
"We are here to release these documents today because for a long time New Yorkers have known the truth, but they have been unable to see the truth in any document presented to them," he added.

Among the documents that have been revealed is the "Harding Memo", an October 2001 memo from then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that indicated the city knew of the air quality dangers and the legal liability even through publicly the city declared the air was safe.
The memo has been sought by 9/11 victims advocates for decades.
Another released document shows the presence of asbestos on the facade ledge of 15 John Street, away from Ground Zero, months after the attacks, in July 2002.

In addition to releasing the first throve of city documents, the city announced a settlement of two lawsuits brought by the advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued the city to force publication of the records.
Nearly 6,000 people have died of 9/11 related illnesses since the attacks and many are suffering from chronic illnesses, according to the group.

Advocacy groups filed several Freedom of Information Act requests for the documents over the years, but it was only last year that 68 boxes of records were found in a city office, according to city officials.

"The Daily Show" host Jon Stewart, who has been advocating for health benefits for 9/11 first responders, said at the news conference that many of those victims had to fight for the documents while they were "sick and dying."

"I'm not saying the information may have changed the outcomes, unfortunately, for their families, but I guarantee you it would not have been the struggle that it was to get people to recognize what they all knew ... that there was poison in the air," he said.

Mamdani declined to directly blame any of his predecessors, saying he would "leave that to New Yorkers," but said, "administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity."

The mayor said that the city will continue to use its resources to promote two federal programs established under the Zadroga Act: the World Trade Center Health Program and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. They are designed to provide relief to residents and workers who were in downtown Manhattan after the attacks if they experience any related illnesses.

title: What Secret Service did immediately after the 9/11 attacks
summary: Agents across the nation scrambled to prevent attacks on U.S. leadership in the wake of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
story: Agents across the nation scrambled to prevent attacks on U.S. leadership.
On Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. Secret Service Director Brian Stafford saw a situation spinning out of control.

In the Secret Service Crisis Center at its Washington, D.C., headquarters, he watched the aftermath of the attacks on World Trade Center, with multiple protectees to ensure the safety of -- including President George W. Bush who was in Florida.
As he called out directions and weighed options, he also considered the possibility of a decapitation attack on United States leadership.

As Stafford quarterbacked the response and monitored protectee locations, he faced the unprecedented responsibility of enacting the federal Continuity of Operations Plan, under Presidential Decision Directive 67, which provides a framework to relocate U.S. leadership to safety.
Not even in World War II had this full continuity posture been activated in this manner, and Stafford had to execute a plan the nation had trained for but never used.

"9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. ET across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
In New York City, Special Agents Tom Armas and John Buckley -- who were at the New York Field Office at 7 World Trade Center for the annual UN General Assembly briefing -- raced into the North Tower.

Nearing the 40th floor, the tower moved and knocked them off their feet due to the shockwave of the South tower being struck. Making their way back down, they became trapped in the lobby as the South Tower collapsed and blew out the windows.

Once the rumbling stopped, Armas -- in gym shorts and a T-shirt with his gear clipped to his belt -- and Buckley led a group of civilians and FDNY members outside. Briefly separated on the street amidst the smoke and debris, they reunited minutes later to continue moving people out of harm's way, the pair recalled in 2021.

In Florida, Deputy Special Agent in Charge Edward "Eddie" Marinzel -- who was Bush's detail leader for the visit -- was compelled into emergency action when White House Chief of Staff Andy Card told him that "America is under attack," Marinzel told Pittsburgh's WPXI in 2011.

Coordinating with Card, the White House military aide and Air Force One advance teams, to get the president away from potential harm, Marinzel and the team settled on Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana for its communications capabilities, countering the president's initial demand to return straight to a vulnerable Washington, D.C.

To keep the Bush moving, Air Force One continued to Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska, headquarters of U.S. Strategic Command (STRATCOM). By coincidence, the base had a nuclear war drill planned that day, making it the safest location possible.
Once notified that civilian airspace was grounded and combat air patrols secured D.C., Marinzel acquiesced to the president's order to return to the capital.

Across Washington, protective details moved instantly to secure leadership. Detail leader Nick Trotta diverted first lady Laura Bush from the Capitol directly to Secret Service Headquarters. While second lady Lynne Cheney was relocated from the American Enterprise Institute back to the White House.

At the White House, Special Agent Jimmy Scott -- who was part of Vice President Dick Cheney's protective detail -- received word of an inbound hijacked plane. He burst into the vice president's office, grabbed him by his shoulder and belt, and propelled him to the underground Presidential Emergency Operations Center bunker to ensure his survival, Cheney said in his 2011 autobiography.

As night fell that day, Secret Service agents across the nation continued to respond with valor and courage. Most made critical decisions in the heat of battle without clear direction or orders, anchored purely in the mission to protect lives.

"On 9/11, we didn't have time to think about our own families until the sun went down," an unnamed Secret Service agent later reflected. "The only thing that mattered was that the chain of command stayed unbroken, the leaders stayed alive, and the country knew someone was still standing guard."
Sept. 11, 2001 -- Never Forget.

Donald J. Mihalek is an ABC News contributor, retired senior Secret Service agent and regional field training instructor who served on the president's detail and presidential transitions. The opinions expressed in this story are theirs and not those of ABC News.

title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
summary: Stephen Siller Jr. spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S.
story: Stephen Siller Jr. was just 9 months old when his firefighter dad died on 9/11.
On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner.
"He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News.

"When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan."
He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old.

Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired.

The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News.

9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful."

At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago."
To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's.
"Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across."

The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many."

As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11.

"And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot."

"Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel."

Siller Jr. found one of the most memorable stops to be Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he learned of the attacks.
"We normally have stairs that go up to the steel truck," Siller Jr. explained, but on this May visit to the school, it was pouring rain.
Still, the children "were begging the firemen, 'Hey, can we get up? We just want to touch the steel,'" Siller Jr. said.
As the kids were lifted up, they began "praying over this steel," he recalled.
"Little kids who understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history ... it once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day," he said.
"I was really shocked at how interested they were," he said.
To Frank Siller and Siller Jr., educating the next generation was a key goal of the Steel Across America campaign.

"These kids were incredible; they were patient ... and they consistently showed up," Siller Jr. said. "No matter where we were in the country, there were families there, which was beautiful -- fathers and mothers wanting to teach their kids."

"I was 9 months old on 9/11 -- if you were born after me, and not in New York City, you know, there's a high chance that you have no real understanding of that day," he continued. "It's important that that lesson is taught to these kids -- there's so much to be pulled from the sacrifices made."

The Steel Across America campaign is part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, started by Frank Siller in honor of his brother's run from the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the World Trade Center. The foundation supports military members, first responders and their families across the U.S. The foundation is currently providing wounded veterans and first responders with mortgage-free, specially-adapted smart homes.
"We didn't let Stephen just perish in that rubble and let that story end there. No, we took his act of courage and sacrifice and said, 'We're going to do good with it,'" Frank Siller said.

"Would Stephen make that run again through the tunnel, knowing he was gonna die? I think he knew he was gonna die," Frank Siller said. "At the very least, he knew it was a strong possibility that he might not be coming home. And to think that he did that, knowing how much he loved Sally and his kids, people like that are few and far between. ... And it's got to be recognized and never forgotten."

title: Meet the chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
summary: In the weeks after the World Trade Center was destroyed, city chefs and thousands of New Yorkers banded together to help feed Ground Zero workers around the clock.
story: Members of "Operation Chefs With Spirit" reflect on the tragedy 25 years later.

Chef Don Pintabona spent years cooking up the finest dishes for celebrities, Wall Street brokers and other VIPs at the Tribeca Grill in downtown Manhattan, but nothing could have prepared him and the rest of the city's restaurant community for their biggest job.

In the hours after the World Trade Center was attacked and destroyed on Sept. 11, 2001, Pintabona said he and many other chefs, caters, food service workers and others all yearned to help the city in some capacity with their skills, but didn't immediately know how.

But through quick thinking, organizing and the generosity of thousands New Yorkers, Pintabona and the other restaurant members put together a massive operation that fed Ground Zero workers around the clock for two months after the attacks.
"Everybody kind of just said, 'Okay, let's jump in,'" Pintabona, 66, told ABC News.

He and other volunteers of "Operation Chefs with Spirit" said that even though 25 years have passed since the attacks, the memories of those weeks are still fresh, as is the sense of awe at how they put the operation together.
Turning the page on a tragedy
Pintabona said he had a desire to do something after the attacks to help the city, but it was a little piece of paper that came to him serendipitously that sparked his idea for the operation.
On Sept. 11, he said he watched the destruction of the towers from the roof of his home in Brooklyn, which was so close that pieces of paper debris from the towers were floating in the air near him.

One of those was a "P" page from a dictionary and when Pintabona picked it up he said he noticed that one side of the page had words with negative connotations, such as pesky, while the other side had words such as persevere, perseverance, persistence.

“9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.

"I mean, in my mind, this came straight from heaven, that through the perversion, you gotta persist, you gotta persevere," he said. "So those words were banging around my head for the days and weeks and just trying to figure out how can I live up to this."

Pintabona said the next day he was able to get to his restaurant, and he started cooking with what he had in his kitchen. He then brought the food to Stuyvesant High School in lower Manhattan, which was one of the staging areas for first responders.
"We had just floods of people coming in to attack the food," he said adding that the meals were gone in a matter of hours.

Pintabona said he wanted to continue to feed more people but transporting the meals through the streets, which were damaged and restricted to first responders and the National Guard, would be a challenge. He said he had a eureka moment during a cigarette break while watching the Hudson River.
"I saw a barge…And I said, 'Holy s---, this is it. We've got to feed everybody by boat,'" he recalled.
A crew assembles, quickly gets into action
Pintabona told ABC News he found that that other chefs in the city were also interested in feeding the Ground Zero workers and they all put their heads together.

He soon started calling up several contacts within the food industry, the city government and the owner of Spirit Cruises, which operated city sightseeing and party cruises lines, and things quickly began to fall in place.

Spirit provided three boats, one at Chelsea Piers that would be used to cook and prepare the meals, another to transport the food to Ground Zero, and a third, a triple decker, stationed in Battery Park City near the pit that was used for the workers to eat and rest.

The city's top chefs, such as Charlie Palmer, Danny Meyer and Daniel Boulud, and food workers and volunteers would be doled out with tasks with everything from cutting veggies to organizing forks, spoons and plates.

Jim Stewart, a longtime food service coordinator who had experience coordinating food operations at the Meadowlands and other big clients, jumped in when Pintabona made the calls for help. Stewart said he too was compelled to do something after the attacks.
"I think at that point, having something to do was sort of helpful, and it gave you some sort of purpose in a very difficult situation," Stewart, 66, a Navy veteran, told ABC News.
Stewart used his connections to secure food from the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, which was still in fridges following the end of that year's U.S. Open.
Stewart and Pintabona estimated that the food from the tennis center could serve 75,000 meals, but that was all eaten within three days.

Fortunately, they weren't the only New Yorkers who were willing to share from their fridges. Stewart recalled how a whole slew of Downtown Manhattan restaurant staff, from small Chinatown restaurants to larger, more elite eateries like the ones under B.R. Guest, were calling him up and ready to offer their food.
"So they would be bringing down enormous amounts of food packages to go. All the cooks from down there, they brought meals for like 200 people without question for a month," Stewart said.
"I would get a call, and they would go, 'At the airport, there's two pallets of beef from Texas.' It was not just New York," Stewart added.
Pintabona said that thousands of New Yorkers arrived at Chelsea Piers ready to volunteer, even those who never cooked a meal in their life.
Although Pintabona had to turn many would-be volunteers away because of space and logistics issues, he said he worked out to tailor their skills to fit the operation.

"When they would come on, I would try to talk to as many as possible. 'Okay, you work at Smith Barney in the accounting department? You know what? We need you to help us inventory the food that comes in off the trucks,'" he recalled. "A lot of people, obviously servers and whatnot, food service people, I would put them front-facing on the buffets, you know what they're used to."

Megan Murphy was a full time bartender at Rue 51 in Manhattan on Sept. 11 and she told ABC News she immediately answered Stewart's call. She helped to serve the food and coordinate with other volunteers right at the pit.

"It was my call to duty," Murphy, 51, told ABC News while holding back tears. " I had been doing something because I was helpless. I felt helpless and I just wanted to help. I just want to be…I just needed to be there."
'Nourishing more than their stomachs'
By Sept. 14, the operation had kicked off and the volunteers were ready to go and the first set of food was delivered to the pit.
The boats would sail from Chelsea Piers nearly 2 1/2 miles south to Ground Zero with a team of volunteers and return back for another round and the operation would continue 24/7.
Workers still had soot on them and looked liked they hadn't slept in days but they gladly accepted the meals and cherished the time to step away from the terrible scene.
Pintabona said massage therapists joined in on the volunteering and provided the crews with free massages to ease their muscles.
He said the meals definitely helped the pit workers have the energy to push through with their work, but the chefs and volunteers all felt that their service meant a lot more than a free lunch.

"You'd see the looks on the faces of people that came in, if they'd been on the pile for God knows how many hours and starving and then they got to sit in a clean environment and then talk to other first responders," he said.
"So that was the most amazing part of the effort," he added, "[It] kind of nourished a lot more than just stomachs."

Murphy, who continued to bartend at night during her volunteer time, said that many who came down to help went beyond just serving food and in many cases offered the pit crews a place to unwind and let out their raw emotions.
"I would make an effort just to go to everyone and talk to them, and let them talk to me about the experience," she said.
"If after lunch they could walk out and I could walk out with them and they were smiling and getting off their shift and made it a better day, that was what I was there to do," Murphy added.
The volunteers and chefs said that while they pushed forward with the operation, with some sleeping on the boats, the stress and hard work did compound.
Fortunately, the volunteers had each other's backs, according to Pintabona and Stewart.
"It got so ridiculous that one day Jimmy was working the phones and, you know I just had this stupid, selfish craving for a Krispy Kreme doughnut," Pintabona recalled.

"I said, 'All right, let's call this guy.' We called them, and the next day a whole truck with like 20 rolling racks of Krispy Kreme donuts showed up," Stewart said. "So [Pintabona] looked at me and was like, I should have known better."
Looking back 25 years later

The operation ended after roughly two months and roughly a million meals after the Red Cross came in and took care of meals for the Ground Zero pit crew. But Pintabona said that the crew didn't grow apart.
He organized a Christmas party at Cipriani in Soho for all of the volunteers and their families and many stayed in touch in the last 25 years.
Stewart said he was humbled by the outpouring of support from not only New Yorkers, but people throughout the world who heard about the feeding operation and were moved.

"I have these pictures that were sent to me from a class where the children, they drew cartoons," he recalled. "They said like, 'Keep going. You're doing great.' You know, 'thank you for your efforts.'"
Murphy said that she is still emotional thinking back to the weeks after the attacks, but the memories of selfless New Yorkers always stand out.
"New York is strong, New Yorkers are strong," she said.
Pintabona agreed and said for him it all came back to that floating dictionary page and that push to persevere.
"You have to turn the page and stay on the positive side. So that's kind of what I've learned through this experience," he said.

title: Trump honors 9/11 victims at the Ellipse, pledging to 'never forget'
summary: President Donald Trump has honored the victims of the Sept_ 11, 2001, attacks by vowing to “never forget.”
story: President Donald Trump has honored the victims of the Sept_ 11, 2001, attacks by vowing to “never forget.”

WASHINGTON -- Nearly a quarter century after a day “etched forever into the memories of Americans,” President Donald Trump honored the victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on Tuesday by vowing to “never forget.”

The event at the Ellipse was spearheaded by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation and showcased a massive, 21-foot, nearly 17,000-pound steel beam recovered from the South Tower of the World Trade Center in New York, which had traveled for months across the country as part of the Steel Across America tour.

The steel beam will make its way through New York in a procession on Friday by retracing the steps of fallen New York City firefighter Stephen Siller. Trump’s presence at the event on Tuesday just outside the White House began a week of commemorations that will culminate in several events on Friday, including one at the Pentagon that Trump will attend.
“This battered piece of steel here today on the Ellipse is a reminder that America is blessed with a strength no fire can consume, no evil can conquer and no terror can destroy,” Trump said.
Trump noted that the Sept. 11 attacks were one of few moments in history that “divide time into really what came before” and after.

His remarks briefly dipped into the political, as Trump warned of people turning a “communistic way” — a reference to his frequent attacks on Democrats as more democratic socialists gain influence in the party.

During his remarks, Trump paid particular tribute to two men who died in the attacks: Jeffrey Palazzo, a New York City firefighter, and Welles Crowther, a young equities trader who became known as the “man in the red bandanna” after rescuing several people in the attacks.

Trump said the U.S. Coast Guard will commission a new fast-response cutter this weekend in New York in honor of Palazzo, a Coast Guard reservist who was working out of Staten Island’s Rescue Squad 5 when he responded to the attacks 25 years ago.
And the president recognized Crowther, also a volunteer firefighter, by awarding him the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
Crowther’s mother, Alison, and sister, Paige, accepted the award, which is considered the nation’s highest civilian honor.
During his remarks, Trump also recalled being near the site after the attacks and hearing the structure then known as the U.S. Steel Building “creaking.”

“I was building a big building in New York and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened," he said. “We thought it was coming down on top of us. And two firemen — big, strong guys, and I’m not the smallest guy in the world -- they grabbed me under the arms."

“They lifted me up and they started running with me,” he added. “I said, ‘Fellas, I could run myself,’ but they were amazing.” It wasn’t clear from Trump’s comments precisely when the event he described occurred.

In attendance were a smattering of top Cabinet officials and members of Congress, including Republican Reps. Mike Lawler of New York and Dan Meuser, whose Pennsylvania district is near Shanksville, where Flight 93 crashed on Sept. 11, 2001.

Trump praised at length Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who was chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a financial firm that had been housed at the World Trade Center. Lutnick lost his younger brother, Gary, as well as more than 650 employees in the attacks.
“He’s done an amazing job,” Trump said of Lutnick. “He’s rebuilt Cantor Fitzgerald, and he’s given much of the profits to some of the families or the families of people who perished.”
About 150 first responders from New York, as well as some from Washington and Pennsylvania, were in attendance, Trump said.

“This steel beam represents the best of our country," said Frank Siller, the foundation’s chairman and CEO who is the brother of Stephen Siller. “It’s important to recognize that the heroism that was exhibited that fateful day was nothing short of incredible.”
Associated Press writer Will Weissert contributed to this report.

title: US tourism groups want to win Canadian visitors back. A testy trade war isn't helping
summary: An acrimonious trade war between the United States and Canada is threatening to reinforce the resolve of Canadians who stopped visiting the U.S. last year
story: An acrimonious trade war between the United States and Canada is threatening to reinforce the resolve of Canadians who stopped visiting the U.S. last year

LAS VEGAS -- Appeals from American tourism organizations seemed to be everywhere Josh Loewen looked over the last year. Billboards and banners proclaimed a state or city's love for Canada. Online and social media ads offered special deals for travelers from north of the border.

As a Vancouver resident and marketing executive himself, Loewen said he understands the conciliatory overtures. The number of Canadians traveling to the United States plunged after President Donald Trump returned to office with remarks about making Canada the 51st state. An acrimonious trade war between the two countries now is threatening to reinforce the informal boycott just as it appeared to be easing slightly.
"It’s such a big ask right now,” Loewen, 45, said of the U.S. tourism industry's attempts to woo Canadians like him back before a new president occupies the White House. “It’s just a wasted effort.”

Relations between the U.S. and Canadian governments have deteriorated sharply since their trade negotiations collapsed last month. Trump imposed import taxes of up to 50% on a range of Canadian products. Canada’s government responded in kind. Trump ordered the U.S. government to change the name of border-spanning Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed insults from members of Trump's Cabinet as childish and undignified.
The bilateral rift has not stopped state and local tourism officials and popular destinations like Graceland from trying to persuade Canadian visitors to return.

New York state launched a “NY Loves Canada” promotion this summer, offering discounts at hotels, restaurants and attractions. Some downtown Las Vegas hotels are treating the Canadian dollar as equivalent to the U.S. dollar to give Canadian visitors more value for their money. Las Vegas tourism officials went to Canada last month to meet with travel advisers, tour operators and airline representatives.
“We’re here to make sure you know that we care about Canada," Steve Hill, president of the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, said while in Vancouver.

The outreach is happening at the national level, too. Brand USA, the U.S. tourism industry’s marketing organization, is bringing its Travel Week trade-event series to Canada for the first time in October, expanding and rebranding an earlier program known as Canada Connect.

Canada traditionally sent more overnight international visitors to the United States than any other country. Amid last year's consumer-led backlash, both same-day trips and longer stays nosedived. Canadian residents made 25% fewer return border crossings and spent about $2.4 billion (CA$3.3 billion) less on travel to the U.S. in 2025 than they had the year before, according to Canada's national statistical agency, Statistics Canada.

The retreat coincided with other headwinds, including a weaker Canadian dollar that made traveling to the U.S. more expensive and rising prices for airfares and hotels. Canadian air travel to the U.S. started declining in September 2023, Statistics Canada data shows.

But the abrupt pullback in stateside travel that accompanied Trump's second presidency and extended into this year signaled “a persistent shift away from the United States by Canadian residents in their travel preferences,” agency analysts said in a July report.

Tentative signs of improvement emerged in May, June and July, when border crossings picked up slightly, the agency reported. The latter two months coincided with the 2026 World Cup, which the U.S., Canada and Mexico cohosted. Canada’s national soccer team competed during the tournament's early weeks, giving some Canadians a reason to head south. Carney attended the final match in New Jersey alongside Trump.

Trips by car accounted for most of the uptick in cross-border traffic, while air travel to the U.S. fell from year-earlier levels in every month through June, Statistics Canada said. The U.S. National Travel and Tourism Office estimates that during the first six months of 2026, Canadians made even fewer overnight visits, which typically generate more tourism spending, than they did during the same period last year.

A day after the World Cup ended, Trump announced that tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods would take effect in 30 days. The White House said the tariffs were intended to address U.S. complaints over Canadian barriers to American-made automobiles, alcohol and dairy.

“You went from this really high, exciting moment for the U.S. in terms of international attention, to the next week, it’s negative again,” said Deborah Friedland, a hospitality consultant at financial services firm Eisner Advisory Group. “It’s one step forward and two steps back.”

With the summer now winding down, some of the U.S. destinations most dependent on Canadian visitors are heading into their most important season. Large numbers of Canadian snowbirds typically flock to warm-weather locations in Florida, Arizona and California when temperatures drop at home, making the coming months a test of whether the grassroots boycott will extend into another winter.
“I’d be surprised if we’re talking a year from now and all of a sudden you see this huge uptick in Canadian travel over the winter months," Friedland said.

Not all tourism officials are worried. Jennifer Adams, tourism director for the Destin-Fort Walton Beach area in Florida’s Panhandle, said she never panicked when headlines about Canadians shunning travel to the U.S. first appeared last year.

“I felt our message was strong," she said, adding that, “the thing for us is to let the Canadian family know that they are welcomed here and we are committed to giving them a great experience when they get here.”

Florida saw a 7% decline in Canadian visitors in 2025 compared to the previous year, according to state marketing organization Visit Florida. Sister organization Visit California, citing data from global research and consulting company Tourism Economics, estimated that Canadian visitation to the Golden State fell 20%.

Loewen, the Vancouver marketing executive, said his family loved visiting the United States. He, his wife and their two children often traveled to San Diego, Portland and Seattle. This year, they chose Mexico instead.

The reluctance, Loewen said, has little to do with whether the U.S. can offer a good vacation. It’s about whether Canadians want to spend their money there while tensions between their country and the U.S. remain so high. Loewen said his family hasn't stepped foot in the U.S. since Trump’s inauguration and doesn't plan to until there's a new president.

Eileen March, a life coach from Calgary, said she made a similar decision. Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st state and his trade policies were part of it, as was a broader sense of no longer feeling safe or welcome in the United States, March said.

“As time has worn on, I was beginning to waver,” she said. The latest round of tariffs “reinforced my initial decision to not travel in the U.S. at all while he is in office." She refuses even to book flights with layovers in the U.S.
March, 41, knows that staying away for four years is a long time. She is prepared to go even longer.
“I think that’ll really depend on who is elected next, their values and the relationship they attempt to foster or repair with Canada,” she said.

title: Travelers flocked to Illinois last year, generating over $88B in economic impact
summary: Illinois tourism reached new heights last year, breaking records in visitor spending and generating over $88 billion in economic impact
story: Illinois tourism reached new heights last year, breaking records in visitor spending and generating over $88 billion in economic impact
Illinois tourism reached new peaks last year, breaking records on visitor spending and generating over $88 billion in total economic impact, Gov. JB Pritzker’s office announced.

The growth was driven by around 115 million domestic and international tourists, who spent $50.2 billion while traveling in Illinois — an increase of 3.5% from the year before, and marking the first time the state has surpassed the $50 billion threshold for visitor spending.

“We’re in the Middle of Everything and there’s something here for everyone — from the beaches of Lake Michigan to the rolling prairies of Southern Illinois,” said Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton. “Illinois has a rich history, culture, and natural beauty and we’re excited to welcome people from near and far to enjoy it all.”
The spending also produced nearly $5 billion in direct state and local tax revenues for Illinois communities and $372 million in hotel tax revenue.

According to a news release from the governor’s office, the state’s ‘Middle of Everything’ tourism campaign helped generate an additional 2.8 million trips and $904 million in visitor spending last year.

Illinois’ tourism industry was also supported by over $3.3 million in state grants in fiscal year 2025, helping to promote projects like the state’s Route 66 centennial celebrations and the Illinois America 250 campaign.
The state’s Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity says it is expanding its focus on outdoor recreation activities with a dedicated unit within its tourism office.

Outdoor recreation activities have been the primary draw for tourism to the southern part of the state in recent years, with visitors taking advantage of hiking, cycling, rock climbing, and ziplining in Shawnee National Forest — and wine tasting at vineyards along five wine trails.
This story was originally published by Capitol News Illinois and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

title: Reckoning looms for golf carts that zip through Rome's crowded historic center
summary: Rome's historic center is facing a golf cart controversy
story: Rome's historic center is facing a golf cart controversy
ROME -- Beneath the splendor of its monuments and ruins, Rome is taking aim at a modern-day chariot: the golf cart.

Hundreds of them have started carrying tourists through the historic center. Even rolling along at a moderate speed, these golf carts have so far outpaced regulation. But the city is mounting a crackdown.

For critics, the carts are running amok, parking illegally, worsening congestion and unlocking another level of overtourism. Some local media invoke sensational language, calling it an “invasion” and saying Rome is being “held hostage by golf carts.”
Advocates argue carts are silent, occupy less space than tourist vans and buses, and don’t choke the air with exhaust that also stains historic monuments.
The Associated Press got a taste of the enmity during a late August ride when a black, eight-seater van pulled up alongside.
“You’re in the middle of the road!” its driver barked. “Move it!”
“Always the same! The road isn’t yours!” the golf cart driver shouted back. Both gesticulated angrily with their free hands, following a time-honored Roman traffic tradition.

Carts like this zip through Rome’s cobblestone alleys, past tourists eating spaghetti carbonara from checkered tablecloths and shops hawking hot priest calendars and tote bags stamped with cliches (Ciao Bella!). But there’s no time to buy anything except a cappuccino or gelato; these tours are targeted blitzes on Rome’s hot spots — at least until they collide with authorities.
Best buckle up.

Ruth Sanderson from Manchester, England, surprised her husband with the tour for his birthday during their first trip to Rome. They could see the major sights in three hours and “just potter around” for the rest of their short stay, said Sanderson, 50.

Their guide swung around the basilica where Pope Francis is buried then headed to the Spanish Steps, where he parked in an area exclusively for car-sharing — the first of several illegal spots he snagged.
“We don’t have a proper stop for golf carts, so we park where we can — as legal as possible,” driver Martin Halili explained to them.
Even before the golf cart boom, parking was a pain. Cars, vans, Vespas and motorcycles are stationed atop curbs, crosswalks and medians. Trucks double-park while unloading.

Any spare cranny is claimed in Rome's historic center, because there are only 4,300 regular on-street spots available, about one-quarter the number of cars owned by the area's residents, according to the city's transport chief, citing a field survey conducted last year. Plus, an average 50,000 vehicles enter daily. Unsurprisingly, some residents are unhappy.

“This was the last straw because, unfortunately, there has already been traffic here for a long time, since there are too many categories of vehicles authorized,” Luigi la Licata, head of the Monti neighborhood association, told the AP. “The golf cart is the most obvious one — and the latest — but there are many others.”

Golf cart bookings this summer grew 147% from 2024, according to TripAdvisor, whose subsidiary Viator is the biggest source of passengers. Rome has as many as 500 carts, with one-fifth belonging to the Metur association of tour operators, established last December to seek common ground with locals and the city.

“Overtourism is a real problem, and we’re not denying it. And maybe we’re also part of it in a way. But if we’re part of it, then at least be part of it in a smart way,” Pascal van Duijnhoven, the association’s president, said. “We believe, especially for Rome, that it’s a solution. And we really hope that people start looking at it like this. But we need a hand. We need some help from the authorities.”
Rome’s deputy mayor for sustainable mobility and transport, Eugenio Patanè, is striving to restore order and reduce traffic — and not just golf carts.

In July, electric vehicles started paying for admission to the historic center, as gasoline-powered cars had been — a strategic shift from cutting emissions to tackling congestion. The number of authorized vehicles is down about one-quarter, to 350,000, and Patanè aims to halve the number of daily entrants.

But it hasn't been so simple to put the brakes on golf carts. First, not all carts are created equal; technical specifications mean some fall under existing rules while others can roam freely. Second, passenger transport and tourism businesses are regulated regionally, Patanè said.

So he requested the region transfer that power to Rome, and anticipates that will occur this month. Then he can present his regulation that would establish fixed tour routes, cap the number of carts of all types and create a system to select operators.

“Cities where this golf cart phenomenon is expanding truly have very few weapons,” he said. “We will be able to regulate this phenomenon that has now become rampant and, in some cases, even worrisome.”
Operators say such proposals would kneecap their nascent industry. Meantime, their carts are already getting curbed.

Authorities stopped vehicles owned by Metur associates 14 times in the back half of August, with reviews of drivers' documents that lasted up to an hour, van Duijnhoven said, and punishments that were inconsistent and severe. Carts allegedly operating as black-market, private-hire vehicles can be banned from the streets for over a month, or drivers slapped with 4,000-euro ($4,600) fines for unlicensed tour guiding.

One block from the Pantheon, the AP saw an officer from Italy's financial police inspecting the documents from a cart carrying a family from Florida. During the half-hour stop, he took their IDs and copied down their information. Three nearby private-hire vans — also parked illegally — were receiving no such scrutiny.
Halili, who guided the couple from Manchester and owns Wheel Tours, says private-hire and taxi drivers are bristling at the new kid on the block taking a bite out of their business.
“They have waged a war against us, filing complaints and appeal after appeal, because they are a powerful lobby,” he said. “This is the problem: They have it in for golf carts.”

title: Temporary protections for about 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants are in limbo as deadline nears
summary: Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador are in limbo as a deadline nears for the Trump administration to decide on ending them, as it has done with hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries
story: Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador are in limbo as a deadline nears for the Trump administration to decide on ending them, as it has done with hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries

MIAMI -- Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador was in limbo Wednesday as a deadline neared for the Trump administration to decide if they should end, as it has done for hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries.

The Temporary Protected Status designation expires Wednesday but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens. If the Department of Homeland Security takes no action, protections are automatically extended for six months. This rare reprieve happened in May, when the protections were automatically extended to about 11,000 Lebanese, allowing them to stay and work in the U.S. for another 180 days.

About 200,000 people from El Salvador have lived in the U.S. since 2001 under TPS, which allows people already in the country to remain with work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months, if the secretary of homeland security determines conditions are unsafe for return. They are eligible for work permits.

During President Donald Trump’s second term, Homeland Security has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 14 countries, including El Salvador, Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. Only about 103,000 from three countries remain protected with termination dates in October for Ukraine and Sudan, and November for Lebanon.

The Trump administration obtained a major victory when the Supreme Court ruled in June that Homeland Security acted within its authority by ending TPS for about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The impact of the decision extends far beyond Haitians and Syrians, potentially affecting nearly 1.3 million people from 17 countries on TPS.
TPS was created by Congress in 1990  to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It was granted to El Salvador following two devastating 2001 earthquakes that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden extended TPS for El Salvador for 18 months to Sept. 9, 2026.

The vast majority of Salvadoran TPS holders have children born in the U.S. Many have lost their jobs and fear being detained, separated from their American family members, and deported to a country they barely know.

El Salvador, once one of the most violent places in the world, has become one of the safest countries in the Americas since Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele ordered mass arrests in 2022. In April 2025, the State Department upgraded El Salvador’s travel advisory to its highest level, citing a drop in violent crimes and murders.
Bukele has been an ally of Trump’s policy of mass deportations and was one of the first countries to receive deportees and held them at a mega prison in El Salvador also known as CECOT.
Human rights groups and advocates have denounced mass and arbitrary arrests, torture, and disappearances in the Central American nation’s prison system.

Trump received Bukele at the White House in April of 2025 and invited him to participate in a military coalition to fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. Less than a year later, in July of 2026, Trump and Bukele met again in Washington, the Salvadoran president has not publicly stated whether he requested an extension of TPS from the Trump administration.
In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Bukele asked Trump to extend TPS. It remained because there were lawsuits.
Salvadorans in the U.S. sent $9.9 billion in remittances to El Salvador last year, representing 24% of country’s gross domestic product, according to El Salvador’s central bank.

title: In North Carolina, a race is on to restore critical peatland before it dries up or is destroyed
summary: Scientists and investors are restoring a 23-square-mile tract of peatland in North Carolina to help curb climate-warming emissions and restore native habitat
story: Scientists and investors are restoring a 23-square-mile tract of peatland in North Carolina to help curb climate-warming emissions and restore native habitat

BELHAVEN, N.C. -- The birds are up with the sunrise — warblers, flycatchers, sparrows and towhees calling across the treetops. Deer browse on tender buds emerging from dense shrubs. Black bears scrounge for roots, insects and other edibles.

It's an idyllic setting in North Carolina's Inner Banks, where fields of cotton, soybeans and corn stretch for miles, country roads wend through stands of pines and thousands of bird watchers converge to witness the spring migration.
But it's what’s underground that has drawn scientists and investors to this 23-square-mile (60-square-kilometer) tract: spongy, dense peat up to 15 feet (5 meters) deep.
They're here to save it.

Fifty miles (80 kilometers) of ditches dug decades ago for an abandoned farming venture drained much of the water from thousands of years of accumulated peat, leaving the site vulnerable to drought and wildfires, altering its native habitats — and allowing it to emit 130,000 tons of climate-warming carbon dioxide a year.

“Our goal is for perpetuity to conserve these lands so they can’t become oil and gas fields, so they’re not mined for phosphorus or turned into parking lots and shopping centers,” said Tripp Wall, CEO of Colorado-based company Pantheon Regeneration. “They’re just these incredible systems that I feel are underappreciated here in the U.S. (that) for 10,000 to 15,000 years have been climatologically resilient until we screwed them up.”

Peatlands are a climate paradox. Though they account for just 3% of global land surface, they store one-third of the Earth’s carbon dioxide, more than all forests combined. But when degraded — primarily when farmers lower the water table to grow crops — destroyed or burned, they become part of the problem, releasing huge volumes of greenhouse gases, now about 6% of the annual global total from all sources.
And the type of peatlands found in North Carolina, and for hundreds of miles along the Eastern Seaboard, are among the most threatened in the world.

Pantheon plans to reverse the damage by blocking off ditches to control the water table and significantly reduce carbon dioxide emissions. Then it will cull invasive species and replant native grasses, flowers and other plants.

The restoration is modeled after other projects by nonprofits and government agencies, including at the adjacent 175-square-mile (453-square-kilometer) Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge — one of the largest peatland restoration projects in the U.S. — which provides habitat for threatened and endangered species such as red wolves, yellow pitcher plants and Atlantic white cedar, and has become an important stopover for migrating birds such as Tundra swans.

But what sets apart Pantheon's project is a plan to sell carbon credits to tech companies and other corporations that want to compensate for their own greenhouse gas emissions, then use the money to restore and preserve a million acres (1,562 square miles, or 4,047 square kilometers) of peatland from Virginia to northern Florida over the next decade.
Each property will be permanently conserved and rewilded — “big corridors, big birding habitats, big biodiversity hotspots that have an outsized impact on climate,” said Wall.
Neal Flanagan pushes a metal tube through roots and around buried logs until it sinks about a meter (3 feet). When he pulls it out, it’s packed with black soil.

Near the surface, it’s dry and full of dead fibers from plants like wood fern, blueberry and Lyonia. The middle is crumbly, moist and odorless, with bits of charcoal from long-ago fires. But the saturated bottom, 50% carbon, is the consistency of axle grease.

“This is the black gold,” said Flanagan’s colleague, Duke University ecologist Curtis Richardson, as ancient peat oozes from his closed fist. Its “magnitude and importance cannot be underestimated,” he added.

When peatlands are intact, gases generated by decomposing plants are trapped in a waterlogged, oxygen-deprived environment, while surface vegetation absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, scientists say.

That makes ancient, intact peatlands a carbon vault up to 50 feet (15 meters) deep in some parts of the world. They also store about 10% of global fresh water, help control flooding and can help stem wildfires.

But two-thirds of temperate peatlands — mostly in Europe and the U.S. — have been dewatered, while about 45% of tropical peatlands have been similarly disturbed, according to a 2025 study published by The Society for Conservation Biology.

Boreal peatlands, or those in colder climates in places like Canada and Russia, are about 90% intact, but face growing pressure from thawing permafrost and intense fires, both linked to climate change, as well as mining and critical minerals exploration.
At the same time, only 17% of global peatlands are officially protected, according to the study.

In the U.S., significant amounts of peat are also found in Alaska, Florida, parts of the Northeast and the northern Great Lakes, though the type of domed peatlands found in North Carolina exist only along the Eastern Seaboard. Called Pocosin peat, it formed from coastal pine forests and evergreen shrubs that decayed over millennia.
In North Carolina alone, 11,000 miles (17,702 kilometers) of canals drain peatlands before the water empties into coastal estuaries, Richardson said.
Combined with climate change, that leaves them vulnerable to the greatest threat to peatlands globally: catastrophic fire.

Blackened tree trunks rise above a marshy area, the only sign that a fire burned almost 2,000 acres (809 hectares) here four years ago, lowering the ground by a foot and a half (0.5 meters) in some places.

It could have been worse, but the North Carolina Forest Service and other agencies extinguished it fairly quickly — in about three weeks — pumping water from nearby lakes to prevent it from spreading into the wildlife refuge, which borders Pantheon’s property on three sides.

A 2008 fire that began during a drought burned for three months above ground and smoldered for another four underground, damaging more than a quarter of the refuge and lowering the ground by several feet in some areas, refuge manager Sarah Toner said. In areas where water-level restoration had begun, though, the fire burned less deeply.

Saturated peatlands are nearly fireproof: Just the surface vegetation and a few inches of peat burn, which releases nutrients, regenerates seed banks and creates beneficial biochar. But when they’re dry, fire can burn underground for weeks or months — drying out and destroying even the saturated layers — emitting enormous volumes of carbon dioxide and destroying thousands of years of accumulation.
“We’ll lose 5, 6 feet of peat in a matter of weeks, which equates to millions of tons of carbon loss — ancient carbon loss that we simply can’t ever get back in human lifetimes,” Richardson said.
That’s why Pantheon is moving quickly to restore the North Carolina site, Wall said. Although the company hopes to also buy intact peatlands, its first priority is drained sites.
“There’s this urgency to start with what’s degraded now,” Wall said, “before it goes away.”

Steve Apfelbaum steers his SUV down grassy, rutted lanes, then hops out to listen intently, occasionally peering through binoculars. He smiles when he hears prairie warblers, a bird whose population is declining.

“We heard hundreds of them today,” said Apfelbaum, a plant and animal ecologist conducting breeding and migratory bird surveys at the site. “What that tells me is that this ecosystem is really important” for the species’ migration.
He hears Nashville warblers that call from the tops of trees, but nest in cavities in the peat.
Peatlands are key to helping preserve bird populations, which are declining across all habitats, said Apfelbaum: “All sorts of cool birds will be back.”

So will native reptiles, plants, fish and insects, said Vladimir Roosevelt, Pantheon's operations director, who's overseeing the restoration. The company already released a pair of red wolves a couple years ago that have since had pups.

Carbon credits work like this: companies, governments or individuals seek to offset their carbon pollution by investing in projects, such as a peatland restoration, that capture carbon. Their effectiveness, however, has been questioned, as over the years some programs have been exposed as exaggerating how much carbon they were capturing or were simply fraudulent.

Pantheon says it's aware of those concerns and guarantees high-quality, scientifically verified credits, based on Richardson's decades of data on carbon loss at the site and ongoing measurements of groundwater levels and the use of sophisticated monitoring equipment, including a tower that measures how much gas is absorbed by and released from the site, as well as computer modeling and core sampling. Those results will be verified by an outside third party.

Investors including Microsoft are providing Pantheon the initial capital to acquire peatland, Wall said. Income from carbon credits — each credit represents a metric ton — will help fund future land purchases.

The changes will be exciting, Apfelbaum said. But everything comes down to first rewetting and restoring the peat, a natural climate solution often overshadowed by other efforts, including reforestation — important, he said, but not as effective.
“We’ve all been bear-hugged and distracted by trees,” Apfelbaum said, “when it’s really soil and peat that hold the most carbon.”
