title: Lithuania training civilians to defend against a Russian invasion
summary: Lithuania is teaching civilians young and old to help defend their tiny nation from a hypothetical Russian invasion, and telling Putin, "We don't fear you."
story: Vilnius, Lithuania — Russia struck Ukraine's capital Kyiv overnight, bringing an end to a three-day pause in attacks by the two countries on each other's capital cities as President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the region to try and broker a peace deal.
At least two people were killed in the Russian strikes on Kyiv.
The neighboring Baltic countries, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — all NATO members — were watching carefully as the U.S. envoys continued their efforts to resolve the four-and-a-half-year war.

But as they watch and hope for peace, Lithuania and its neighbors have also long been preparing for the possibility that continental Europe's first land war in three generations could spread to their doorsteps.

CBS News visited an ordinary high school in Vilnius where, in addition to math class, students were learning military-style survival skills. Along with the rest of their country, they're preparing for the possibility of Russia launching an invasion.
"Today we're working on survival training, and we're going to learn about weapons later," said Neda, a 15-year-old ninth grader.
If there is a crisis, Neda said she would likely put her first-aid knowledge to use and try to become a medic.
Lithuania, which has a population of less than 3 million, slightly smaller than greater Minneapolis, is also training up adult civilians.
History professor Mindaugas Nefas has been learning weapons skills. He told CBS News the whole-of-society approach to national readiness sends an important message.
"I think it's a good example, for Russia not to do anything against Lithuania," because it shows not just the military, but all Lithuanians are "preparing to defend our country," he said.
Taking on board lessons learned in Ukraine, Lithuania's preparations include teaching ordinary people how to use drones — and how to shoot them down.

The nation's small professional military is also embracing the new high-tech tools of war pioneered in Ukraine, including networks of sensors and drones known as the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative that, paired together, are intended to slow any theoretical Russian invasion to a crawl.
But old-school defenses still matter, too, including obstacles meant to stop tanks and command posts buried underground across the tiny nation.

Vilnius, Lithuania's capital city, is less than 20 miles from the border with close Russian ally Belarus, which Vladimir Putin's forces used as a launchpad for their ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But despite that proximity, and Russia's belligerence toward Ukraine's NATO neighbors, Lithuania's Minister of Defense Robertas Kaunas told CBS News he was confident.
He said his nation's message to Russia was clear: "We don't fear you. We understand who are you, and we don't fear you."
The former Soviet Union's occupation of Lithuania only ended when the communist bloc collapsed in 1991, so it is still fresh in the nation's collective memory.
"We are not afraid, because we remember our history," said Kaunas. "We are in our home and we will protect our home."

Until very recently, NATO planners were doubtful that Lithuania could be defended at all against a full Russian assault, given its size and location sandwiched between Russian and Russian-allied territory.
But the technological innovations of the war in Ukraine — and the resilience of the Ukrainian people —   have inspired new hope in the Baltic state.

title: 25 years after 9/11, Taliban rules Afghanistan again, but with U.S. firepower
summary: CBS News finds Taliban forces patrolling Kabul in American armored vehicles, wearing American tactical gear and carrying American weapons.
story: Kabul — As Americans reflect this week on the 25 years that have passed since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, CBS News has returned to Afghanistan, where the war those attacks triggered ended five years ago with the Taliban's stunning return to power.

When the last U.S. and allied soldiers left after a brutal two-decade war, the Taliban's fighters seized billions of dollars worth of American-purchased military hardware. President Trump, whose first administration negotiated the deal to end the war with the Taliban, has accused the Biden administration of "totally botching" the withdrawal.

Five years later, the hardware of America's longest-ever war is still easy to spot on the streets of Kabul. Taliban fighters patrol in armored vehicles once supplied to Afghan forces, wearing American tactical gear and carrying American weapons.
CBS News saw one Humvee in the Afghan capital still adorned with a faded Green Bay Packers decal — a remnant from its past operators.

President Trump has been fiercely critical of the former Biden administration, accusing his predecessor of allowing the U.S. military to abandon billions of dollars in military hardware. Mr. Trump has demanded that the Taliban hand it back.
But the Taliban has proudly shown off its American-funded arsenal, even staging military parades through Kabul's streets.
Pentagon figures released last year show some $7 billion in hardware and weaponry fell into the group's hands when the Afghan National Army collapsed.

Shortly after the 2021 withdrawal, CBS News filmed as "Badri 313," an elite Taliban special forces battalion, patrolled in their American vehicles, American commando gear and with their American weapons.

Asked about President Trump's determination to reclaim the equipment, Taliban Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News the hardware now belongs to "the state of Afghanistan, and we are not in the business of doing transactions and deals on the assets of the state of Afghanistan."

When it was pointed out that American taxpayers purchased the equipment, Balkhi said: "The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?"
The Taliban waged a vicious insurgency during a war that killed more than 2,400 U.S. service members and tens of thousands of innocent Afghans.

But critics of the Biden administration's handling of the U.S. withdrawal say it's allowed the Taliban to transform from insurgents into a state military force armed with billions of dollars in American-funded firepower.

They have used those weapons to impose a draconian interpretation of Islamic rule on Afghanistan's people, almost completely depriving women and girls of the right to work and study, and restricting life for everyone in the country in ways that some analysts say are even harsher than during the group's previous reign.

Biden has offered little public commentary on the Afghanistan withdrawal, but he said in September 2021, a month after the Taliban took back control, that he "was not going to extend this 'forever war,' and I was not extending a 'forever exit.'"

"If anything, the developments of the past week reinforce that ending U.S. military involvement in Afghanistan now was the right decision," said the then-president in August 2021, as the Taliban reasserted their rule 20 years after being ousted by the U.S.-led military campaign. "American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves."

In 2023, the Biden White House released a 12-page summary of a classified review of the Afghanistan exit that largely blamed the Trump administration for the deal it struck with the Taliban to withdraw U.S. forces from the country by May 2021.

The so-called Doha Agreement brokered by the first Trump administration laid out a series of conditions for the Taliban to fulfill in order for U.S. forces to leave. Another report partially declassified and released by the State Department in 2023 faulted both the Trump and Biden administrations for "insufficient" planning surrounding the withdrawal.

title: King says Prince Harry and Meghan remain private citizens after U.K. return
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan stepped down as senior working members of the royal family in January 2020, and this position, the letter said, "will continue to be fully respected."
story: King Charles III said in a letter Monday that Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, remain private citizens upon their return to the United Kingdom last month.

Charles, who authorized the letter's release to "help avoid doubt or confusion," said the couple are no longer working members of the royal family and will not use the titles "His or Her Royal Highness."

Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, stepped down as senior working members of the royal family in January 2020, and this position, the letter said, "will continue to be fully respected."
The letter said that any security issues are the responsibility of relevant police agencies and the couple's charity work will be carried out in a private capacity.
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," said the letter, sent on behalf of the king by the Lord Chamberlain.
Palace sources suggested it was better to make the letter public, in a spirit of transparency, rather than risk it emerging in leaks.

News broke in late August that Harry and Meghan would be returning to Britain after six years in California. CBS News partner BBC News reported on Aug. 26 that the couple had arrived in the U.K. and are expected to live in the affluent Cotswolds region, about a two-hour drive west of London.
The pair's decision to step away from the royal family and move to California fueled considerable tension with other members of the family.

Harry lost a 2024 legal challenge against a government body's decision to downgrade his security detail on visits back to the U.K., following the announcement that he was stepping away from royal duties.
Harry and Meghan have two children, Archie, born in 2019, and Lilibet, born in 2021.

title: Senior aides to U.K.'s Nigel Farage step down in scandal over undercover report
summary: Two senior aides to Nigel Farage, the firebrand leader of the U.K.'s populist Reform party, have stepped down in the wake of an investigative news report.
story: Two senior aides to Nigel Farage, the firebrand leader of the U.K.'s populist Reform party, have stepped down after the party was accused of breaking British electoral law concerning foreign funding in the wake of an investigative news report where a journalist posed as a wealthy American's son who wanted to donate to the party.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the party said it was launching an internal probe after the report aired on Britain's Channel 4 news late Thursday. Two Reform party officials, James Orr and Dan Jukes, have left their positions pending the outcome of that investigation, the spokesperson said.

"The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing," the spokesperson said.

Jukes is widely regarded as Farage's right-hand man, with an "innate sense of his boss' instinct," according to CBS News' partner network BBC News. Orr, an influential figure in the British national conservative movement, served as Reform's head of policy until his resignation. He is a theologian and associate professor of the philosophy of religion at the University of Cambridge. Both men denied any wrongdoing.
In an interview with a London radio station early Friday, Farage insisted the party had broken no laws.

"The party has not taken any dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever," Farage told LBC Radio. "However, it is a clear case of entrapment, and they worked at it for a very long time, and they got a couple of our contractors to say things that perhaps should not have been said. And as a result of that, they have been removed this morning and yeah, you know, I'm not happy about it."
Channel 4 stood by the report, with a spokesperson telling BBC News the investigation "has been rigorously verified to ensure accuracy. We would encourage people to watch the investigation in full."

The allegations pile further pressure on Farage just as his party's annual conference was getting underway. It also unfolds against the backdrop of scrutiny over donations linked to the party, including an ongoing parliamentary investigation over a multimillion-pound donation from cryptobillionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024. Farage denies any wrongdoing.
Speaking to CBS News at the party's conference, Zia Yusuf, a spokesperson for domestic affairs, downplayed any immediate blowback the allegations would have on the party's internal operations.

"Look, Reform has had many great people who have helped get us to where we are. And I have no doubt, given the talent pipeline that I do have visibility of, both at parliamentary level, potentially, and beyond it, we will withstand this, and ultimately, ultimately will come out strong on the other side," Yusuf said.

On Thursday night, Channel 4 aired the investigation that it said was carried out by an undercover team of journalists from a group called Verbatim, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting.

The investigation follows one journalist who poses as the British-educated son of a wealthy American businessman from Wyoming, who both appeared eager to support the party, which shares aspects of ideology and policy positions with elements of the MAGA movement, as well as other right-leaning populist movements around the world.

British law regards a permissible donor to a U.K. political party as either a U.K.-registered voter or a company. In the scenario that unfolds in the undercover investigation, the son is a permissible donor, and the father is not.

Secretly filmed footage purports to show the two party aides arranging donations from the undercover journalist to fund the commissioning of a number of political polls. According to Channel 4, the donations added up to 32,500 British pounds, which is about $44,000.

Some of those polls later appeared in news articles for British newspapers such as The Telegraph and the Times of London. The articles, which reflect favorably on the party on issues such as its fortunes in local elections and support among labor union members, do not mention how Reform allegedly commissioned the polls.
Jukes is heard telling the undercover journalist that the donation made a "huge impact" for the party while not "showing up anywhere in public records."

Orr denied Reform's involvement in the polling, saying in a video posted to social media an "independent person had paid an independent pollster." "No money reached Reform UK at all, no donation reached Reform UK at all — whether it was in cash or in kind," he said.

The investigation also includes a discussion between Jukes and the journalist on how to circumvent electoral law to secure a separate foreign donation to the party of 500,000 British pounds, or about $675,000. Channel 4 says that donation was never made.
The investigation culminates in a four-way lunch between the journalist posing as the son of the American businessman, an actor playing the businessman, Jukes and Farage.

During that meeting, Farage appears to have knowledge that the funding for the polls came from the businessman, and does not appear to be concerned when the son proposes the method by which the 500,000-pound foreign donation could reach the party, saying, "Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you."
Jukes released a statement to BBC News calling the report "entrapment over a prolonged period of nearly a year by foreign-funded climate change activists."
"I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name," Jukes said.

In a statement to Sky News, Orr said, "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully."
At least two of Reform's opponents, the ruling Labour Party and the centrist Liberal Democrats, have written to the Metropolitan Police, alleging breaches of electoral law.
In a statement to CBS News, the police said it was aware of reporting "involving political party donations" and alleged breaches of British law relating to polling.
The police have not launched an investigation so far, saying it would "assess the matter and any information provided to us."
The U.K.'s Electoral Commission, which regulates party and election finance, confirmed it was in contact with the police.

"The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500," the commission said. "Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."

"Fortunately, enough of me held to the light and that just the crack where it got in was dangerous," Stone added.

"When I was first home from the hospital, I couldn’t sleep at night, and I was sleeping in the day," Stone remembered. "When I was laying on the couch, sleeping and awake, these orbs sort of presented themselves to me. These five orbs presented themselves to me and they sort of talked to me, but in a digital language."

She admitted that she had never previously spoken about the experience because she found it almost impossible to explain. Stone said that she believed the encounter carried a premonition that she would soon lose custody of her then one-year-old son Roan.

"I just kept saying to them, ‘I don’t know if I’m supposed to stay here or if I’m supposed to die,’" Stone recalled of her conversation with the orbs. "And they said, ‘You’re supposed to stay.’ And I said, ‘I can only stay if two of you will stay with my son. Because I don’t want him to be alone, and I think he’s gonna get taken from me.’"

"Sure enough, he was taken from me," she continued. "And I said, ‘We have to have an agreement. The two of you will stay with him and protect him.’ And they agreed. And they said, ‘But your destiny requires that we stay with you.’"

Stone later adopted sons Laird and Quinn, now both 20, as a single mother.

Brandi Glanville is opening up about a series of complex medical diagnoses and the staggering cost of treating a painful condition that has affected her face.

summary: Sandra Bullock reveals her sister's urgent warning forced her to confront the hidden toll of caregiving during partner Bryan Randall's private ALS battle.
story: Quinton Aaron shared what he loves about Sandra Bullock and why he believes they'll always have a connection.
A sobering warning from Sandra Bullock’s sister became a wake-up call for the actress as she quietly navigated her late partner Bryan Randall’s battle with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
Bullock reflected on how caring for Randall through his illness forced her to recognize her own limits – and ultimately ask for help after years of putting others first.

"I'm always a caretaker," she said during an appearance on "Good Hang with Amy Poehler." "Always. And I learned that I didn't take care of the person that was taking care of everybody else. And that was a big wake-up call for me. And I'm not good at asking for help, but I needed help and I needed to ask it in a way that was safe."

She also credited her sister with ringing a much-needed alarm, warning that she needed to start taking care of herself so she could continue being there for her children, Louis and Laila.
Bullock said her sister warned her: "If you do not start taking care of you, something’s gonna happen to you."

"I didn't want to say anything out of turn on what anyone else experienced within that situation, because everyone is experiencing something, their own journey with that," she explained. "There's so much to the story that would be of service. But my story, my slice of pie – and me and the kids, you know – that's all we can speak about."

title: Skillet's John Cooper says woke activists have 'big hearts' but are 'hurting themselves'
summary: Skillet musician John Cooper gets candid about about how wokeness can harm people and explains why he doesn't believe in cancel culture.
story: John Cooper of Skillet told Fox News Digital that he doesn’t think any style of music has "inherent evil," and he believes God gave everyone creative expression.
Skillet frontman John Cooper believes people labeled "woke" are often motivated by good intentions — but warned their approach can ultimately "hurt society."

"I think it’s really worth mentioning that people that we would call woke, the things that we find really problematic, I think it's worth mentioning that most of those people really have big hearts," Cooper said during a recent appearance on the "Unashamed with the Robertson Family" podcast. "They want justice. They want the world to be better."
"They’re just going about it in a way that they don’t know is wrong, and it’s actually hurting them," he continued. "It’s hurting everybody. It hurts society."
SKILLET’S JOHN COOPER SAYS CHRISTIANS WHO CALL ROCK MUSIC ‘DEMONIC’ ARE ‘GETTING THE GOSPEL WRONG’
Skillet frontman John Cooper spoke out about people he considers "woke." (Getty Images)

He said that inner cities in particular are "getting so much worse," saying, "I look at the things that the politicians that say they want to help the poor, they want to help the marginalized, they want to help people of color, whatever it may be, and all they do is keep hurting them more and more and more."
BRANTLEY GILBERT SLAMS ARTISTS WHO BACK OUT OF PATRIOTIC SHOWS UNDER HEAT
Cooper said he believes that "the woke probably have good intentions," and pointed to people he knows personally as proof.
John Cooper is seen performing with Skillet on Sept. 6, 2026 in Dyersville, Iowa. (Tim Mosenfelder/Getty Images)

"I know these people. Some of them work for me. They’ve worked for me for 15 years. I love them," he said. "And I say to them, ‘I know you’re trying to be a good person, but it’s going to hurt people.’"
The musician ultimately attributed his disagreement with those views to his Christian faith.

"What they’re doing is not true, and it’s not based on the Bible," Cooper said. "It goes against the way God tells us how to live. They end up hurting themselves, and now we've got a culture so nihilistic that doesn't know that they matter. They're looking to matter by doing social justice, but they keep hurting themselves more."

Cooper, who has been performing with Skillet for roughly 30 years, recently told Fox News Digital that his Christian beliefs have influenced some of his professional decisions. However, he remains a steadfast supporter of artistic freedom.

"I am a huge believer in freedom of speech," Cooper said. "I hate cancel culture. I don’t want anybody to be canceled because I’ve never said, ‘So-and-so rock artist sings a song against Jesus and I want him pulled down from Spotify.’"
"I would never say that, because that’s not what art is," he added.
Cooper said he has shared the stage with artists who are atheists and even those who openly oppose Christianity.

"Some of them, I would say, are probably personally not only atheist, they probably personally are a little anti-Christ," he said. "And they would know it. They would say, ‘The truth is, John, I just hate the concept of Jesus.’ And we’re still friends."

"I can only think of two things in my entire career I’ve turned down," he said, recalling a band that planned to feature "Jesus on an upside-down cross" during its stage show.

"I don’t think I want to tour with that act," Cooper said. "And it’s not because I hate them. I don’t hate them at all. I’m not calling for them to be pulled down from Spotify. I just go, ‘Hey, this is just something that you’ve gone a little too far to desecrate something that I think is sacred.’"

title: Prince George follows Prince William's footsteps at Eton in a changing royal world: experts
summary: Prince George arrived at Eton College with Prince William and Kate Middleton beaming beside him, marking a major milestone for the future king.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.
Prince George is following in his father's footsteps by attending Eton College and royal experts are calling it a very different royal world.
On Monday, George was photographed arriving on his first day with his happy parents in tow. Prince William and Kate Middleton were seen beaming in photos with their oldest son.

"A new successful chapter for the future heir to the throne. His great-grandmother would be tickled pink. It’s four years to the day, she passed. No doubt he’ll settle in well and master all the skills of kingship," Helena Chard, British broadcaster and photographer, told Fox News Digital.
Prince George (L) and Prince William both photographed at Eton College. (Kensington Palace/Getty Images)

Chard added, "A buoyant Prince George arrived at Eton with the grounding presence of his chuffed supportive parents. He beamed to cameras fully aware of the drill. A brief photo-call, picture release and a hope that his education will take place away from public eyes. Simon Henderson welcomed Prince George to Eton, telling him, 'Welcome. Good Luck. Enjoy it.'"
PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE WON’T ‘HIJACK’ PRINCE GEORGE’S HISTORIC ETON DEBUT, ROYAL EXPERT SAYS
Chard told Fox News Digital that Prince George's classmates could turn into paparazzi, but it's highly unlikely.
Prince George begins his first day at Eton College in Windsor, Berkshire. (Matt Porteous / Kensington Palace)

"A new successful chapter for the future heir to the throne. His great-grandmother would be tickled pink. It’s four years to the day, she passed. No doubt he’ll settle in well and master all the skills of kingship."
"His friends could be the new paparazzi with their phones at the ready. However, my hunch is his peers are of similar high profile ilk, unfazed by celebrity and royalty," she said.
Hilary Fordwich, British royals expert, explained that Prince George is continuing the family tradition by attending Eton.
Kate Middleton and Prince William walk with their 13-year-old son, Prince George, as he arrives for his first day at Eton College on Sept. 8. (Getty Images)

"Just as Prince William attended Eton, it will provide stability, continuity and, given family tradition has proven well for Prince William, it certainly is the best choice given the challenges of raising the future king," Fordwich told Fox News Digital.
Fordwich acknowledged the large media presence for Prince George's first day, she predicts that will die down.
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON 'CAUTIOUS' ABOUT WHICH ROYAL APPEARANCES THEIR CHILDREN MAKE: SOURCE

"While there was extensive coverage of Prince William’s first day, Prince George’s is expected to be more modest with a limited press pool. Given Adelaide Cottage is close by on the Windsor estate, just as Prince William would take tea with his beloved grandmother Queen Elizabeth II, Prince William may well be able to pop home for family visits," she said. "Importantly, being amongst pupils of his ilk he’ll be focused on academics, athletics and relatively normal school-boy adolescent life rather than isolated as previous generations were in the confines of a palace with tutors."

"A new successful chapter for the future heir to the throne. His great-grandmother would be tickled pink," British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. (Matt Porteous / Kensington Palace)
Prince William at Eton College. (Tim Graham/Photo Library via Getty Images)

"Luckily, given the family stability, he won’t be subject to the intense media scrutiny his grandparents went through given the state of their marriage when Prince William attended as then-Prince Charles and Princess Diana’s marriage was rapidly disintegrating," Fordwich added.
Eton College Chapel is the main place of worship for students at Eton College, a famous English boys' school. (Mark Kerrison/In Pictures via Getty Images)

Kate Middleton, Prince William and Prince George arriving at Eton College. (Getty Images)

"I think Prince William and Catherine have been incredibly thoughtful in allowing Prince George to be a child before he has to be a king. Obviously, there is nothing completely normal about being second in line to the throne, but they have surrounded him with routine, family, sports, and school rather than constantly reminding him of his future responsibility," she began.

"Just as Prince William attended Eton, it will provide stability, continuity and, given family tradition has proven well for Prince William, it certainly is the best choice given the challenges of raising the future king," Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. (Matt Porteous / Kensington Palace)

"Eton is a significant new chapter, but I suspect their priority remains the same," Schofield continued. "George should understand who he is without allowing that title to become his entire identity. They cannot give him a completely ordinary childhood, but they can give him a childhood, and I think they have worked very hard to protect that."
WATCH: Prince George earned Eton College spot with 'no special treatment': expert
Due to Eton's high-profile student base, it is possible for Prince George to not be given special treatment, according to Schofield, but he will never just be "another student."

"To a degree, yes. But Prince George will never truly be 'just another student,' because everyone knows who he is and what his future holds," she said. The novelty of having a prince in the classroom eventually wears off when everyone has homework due the next morning."

Pamela Anderson paid a steep price to beat hepatitis C.
After living with the disease for years, the 59-year-old actress said she drained her bank account to pay for an early treatment that insurance didn’t yet cover.

Anderson opened up about her battle with hepatitis C and the shame she carried after her diagnosis in the late '90s while accepting amfAR’s Award of Courage on Sunday in Venice. The nonprofit, which works to end the HIV/AIDS epidemic, also supports hepatitis C research and advocacy.

Anderson went public with her diagnosis in 2002 and claimed she contracted the disease while sharing needles with her ex-husband, Tommy Lee. The Mötley Crüe drummer has denied Anderson's claim.
When a cure eventually became available, Anderson said getting access required a major financial sacrifice.

"Ten blurry years later, there was a cure. I was lucky," she said. "I was offered it in its early stages, and it took everything I had in my bank to pay for it. It wasn't covered by insurance yet, and I felt tremendous guilt that others weren't granted the same access."

title: Prince Harry finds way to live ‘half-in, half-out’ life Queen Elizabeth refused to endorse: experts
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return with their children echoes the "half-in, half-out" proposal Queen Elizabeth II rejected at Sandringham.
story: Hugo Vickers, author of "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History," details how the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit and Oprah interview added strain during the late monarch's final years.
Prince Harry may have finally found a way to live the life that his grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, refused to endorse.

On Sept. 8, 2022, Britain's longest-reigning monarch died after 70 years on the throne. She was 96. On Aug. 26 this year, Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle, returned to the U.K., where their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, will attend school.

As the Sussexes settle into their new life in Britain, with details about their private home and their children's school closely guarded, royal experts told Fox News Digital that the arrangement recalls the "half-in, half-out" proposal the late queen rejected.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex watch a flypast to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London, England. The couple stepped back as senior royals in 2020. They returned to the United Kingdom before Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet started school in September 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Harry may feel vindicated because, superficially, he has created something resembling the freedom he originally wanted," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "But I think calling it a victory misunderstands what the queen rejected."

"I see absolutely no reason to believe she would have changed her mind," Schofield said. "Queen Elizabeth spent 70 years protecting the distinction between the crown and the individual. It seems unlikely that one of the defining judgements of her final years would suddenly have become negotiable."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, leave a service of thanksgiving for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II at St. Paul's Cathedral in London on June 3, 2022, during Platinum Jubilee celebrations marking the monarch's 70 years of service. (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

While the Sussexes have returned to the U.K. for an extended stay, they won't resume their roles as working royals. On Monday, the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, sent a letter to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king's personal representatives around the country.
The letter drew a firm line around the Sussexes’ homecoming, reaffirming that the couple will not resume official duties.

"This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected."

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex," the letter added. "Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020 after describing intense scrutiny from the British press and saying they lacked support from the palace.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital the queen drew a firm line before the couple's departure, insisting the Sussexes could not be "half in, half out" as working royals.

"Her position was simply stated as ‘all in or all out,’" Fordwich said. In his memoir "Spare," Harry recalled the Sandringham meeting and wrote that he believed the royals would consider five options for the Sussexes. "Option Five" called for a full departure. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the palace made a mistake by rejecting the proposal outright.

"The queen had already learned the dangers of ‘half in, half out’ long before Harry and Meghan proposed it," she explained.

title: Christine Taylor was asked to lose 10 pounds after landing Marcia Brady role in 'Brady Bunch Movie'
summary: Christine Taylor revealed she was asked to lose 10 pounds for her role as Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie" during the "Office Ladies" podcast.
story: "The Brady Bunch" stars Barry Williams and Christopher Knight share how they’ve stayed connected over 55 years since the show’s debut.
Christine Taylor landed her dream role as Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie" – but the part came with a catch.

The "Brady Bunch Movie" star recalled the uncomfortable demand she received after landing the role of Marcia Brady during the "Office Ladies" podcast, revealing she was "embarrassed" but agreed to do it because "that was just how things went" in Hollywood at the time.
Taylor landed the role of Marcia after starring in a live show called "The Real Live Brady Bunch."
The actress had been obsessed with Marcia Brady for years and had seen "every single episode ... backwards and forwards, inside out."
MICHELLE PFEIFFER SAYS SHE FELT 'HUMILIATED' FOLLOWING HER AUDITION FOR HER BREAKTHROUGH ROLE IN 'GREASE 2'
Christine Taylor revealed she was asked to lose 10 pounds after landing the role of Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie." (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"And then out-of-the-blue one day, I mean, out of the blue on my answering machine in 1990, whatever year this was, 92 or 93, I got a message from Sherwood Schwartz calling me, just cold calling me saying, 'I would love to meet with you...'" she recalled.
For Taylor, getting a personal call from "The Brady Bunch" creator was the kind of Hollywood moment she never expected – and one she wished she had preserved.
"It was a pinch me moment that I cannot believe to this day that I still didn't keep my little tape from the answering machine," she added.
But beneath the disbelief, Taylor said she had no doubts about whether she was right for the role.
‘BRADY BUNCH’ STAR SHARES THE SIMPLE WORD THAT SAVED HER FROM HOLLYWOOD TRAPS
Christine Taylor said she was "embarrassed" by the request but agreed because that was common in Hollywood at the time. (Getty Images)
"I knew it in my core that there was nobody who could do it better than me," Taylor remembered.
That confidence appeared to carry her through the casting process, which Taylor remembered as surprisingly straightforward.
"I'm fairly sure that I met with them and that was pretty much it," she recalled. "They didn't tell me I got it, but I never had to go back in and audition solo again."
Instead, Taylor read with different actors who would later portray her siblings – Jan and Cindy.

But Taylor said the role also came with a request that reflected a much different era in Hollywood."...It was a very different time in the industry," Taylor explained of the 90s era. "The one thing that I got, and I was not a super heavy person, but they asked me to lose 10 pounds."
Taylor emphasized that she wasn't heavy at the time, but said dropping the weight felt like just another requirement of getting the job.

"But I was like, 'I'll do it.' And then the joke is over the course of the movie, which if you watch it very closely, I start to put the 10 pounds back on, and you can see it," Taylor recalled. Like I'll come into a scene looking a little rounder. And then like I exit the scene looking a little thinner just because of how they had to reshoot things."

title: Barbara Eden, 95, says she’s ‘okay’ after last-minute cancelation of festival appearance
summary: Barbara Eden reassured fans after a "sudden illness" forced her to miss the Cinecon Classic Film Festival, revealing a new medication's side effects.
story: Singer-songwriter Pat Boone reflects on his friendship with country music legend Dolly Parton, who died at 80, on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

Barbara Eden sparked concern among fans after abruptly dropping out of a Los Angeles film festival due to what was described as a "sudden illness," but the 95-year-old actress later shared a reassuring update on social media.
The "I Dream of Jeannie" star was set to be honored during the Cinecon Classic Film Festival at the Landmark Nuart Theatre on Saturday but pulled out shortly before the event was scheduled to begin.
"We’re sorry to share that, due to a sudden illness, Barbara Eden will no longer be able to appear in person at Cinecon tonight," festival organizers announced in a Facebook post on Saturday.
Barbara Eden assured fans that she is "okay" after suddenly pulling out of a scheduled film festival appearance. (Getty Images for Project Angel Food's Lead with Love 7)
ROD STEWART CALLED 'TONE-DEAF' FOR ATTENDING WORLD CUP GAME A DAY CANCELING CONCERT DUE TO HEALTH ISSUES
"Barbara is deeply regretful that she had to cancel at the last minute, as she had been very much looking forward to seeing everyone and celebrating with us," they continued.
"We know how many of you were excited to welcome Barbara. We appreciate your understanding and join you in sending her our best wishes for a speedy recovery," they added.
'YOU'RE SO VAIN' SINGER CARLY SIMON SAYS PARKINSON'S AND CANCER DIAGNOSES KEPT HER FROM PUBLIC EYE
Eden later took to Instagram to clarify the circumstances around her absence and update fans on her condition.
The 95-year-old actress said she was "not suffering from an illness." (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for Project Angel Food's Lead with Love 7)

"It’s okay everyone! I’m okay!" she wrote alongside a photo in which she was seen standing in front of a painting and smiling. "Oh, my goodness there has been a bit of miscommunication," Eden continued. "I’m not suffering from an illness; my doctor very recently prescribed a brand-new medication that turned out to have some nasty side effects. MAYIM BIALIK DETAILS 'NIGHTMARE' AFTER ONE INJECTION OF GLP-1 DRUG LED TO WEEKS OF DEBILITATING SIDE EFFECTS
"What awful timing for this to happen! My deepest appreciation to everyone for the concern," she added. "This is just a speedbump! I expect to be out and about as soon as I’m given the go-ahead!"
"Again, my love and thanks to everyone for all the concern," she concluded.
Cinecon is a classic film festival in Los Angeles that celebrates vintage movies, rare screenings and stars from Hollywood’s Golden Age. This year’s Cinecon marked the festival’s 62nd edition.
CURATORS AT LIBRARY OF CONGRESS DISCOVER LOST FILM BY LEGENDARY CINEMA PIONEER AFTER SPOTTING 'SUBTLE CLUE'

title: Weight regain after obesity drugs tied to higher odds of suicidal thoughts in observational study
summary: Weight-loss drug users who regained weight had 4.2 times higher odds of suicidal ideation, according to a study analyzing data from over 27,000 adults.
story: Bonnie Mitchell, a licensed professional clinical counselor in California, said that while a new study shows a correlation between weight-loss drug use and self-reported mental health symptoms, it cannot prove causation.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Adults who reported using prescription weight-loss medication in the last year had higher rates of depression, mental-health counseling, suicidal thoughts and suicide-related behaviors compared to people who did not take the drugs, according to an observational study.
The research, conducted at Asan Medical Center in South Korea, analyzed data from 27,741 adults (10,908 men and 16,833 women).
Of these participants, 846 had been taking prescription medications for weight control during the previous year, while 26,895 did not take them.
OZEMPIC USERS MAY BE MAKING A MAJOR WEIGHT-LOSS MISTAKE, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS
The weight-loss drug users were 1.9 times more likely to experience depression and twice as likely to seek mental health counseling.
They were also 2.7 times more likely to have suicidal thoughts and 1.7 times more likely to make a suicide attempt.

Adults who reported using prescription weight-loss medication in the last year had higher rates of depression, mental-health counseling, suicidal thoughts and suicide-related behaviors compared to people who did not take the drugs, according to an observational study. (iStock)
The associations were stronger among those using the medications who gained or regained weight.

"The tendency for depression and suicide-related indicators to increase as weight rebounds after using weight-loss drugs may reflect not only the neuropsychiatric effects of the drugs themselves, but also a complex interplay of psychological and social factors associated with failed weight control," the research team wrote in the study.
PATIENTS TAKING WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS OFTEN MAKE 5 CRITICAL MISTAKES, DOCTOR WARNS
The findings were published in the Korean Journal of Family Practice on Aug. 23.
Bonnie Mitchell, a licensed professional clinical counselor in California, noted that this was an observational, cross-sectional study.
The associations were stronger among those using the medications who gained or regained weight. (iStock)

"It shows a correlation between weight-loss drug use and self-reported mental health symptoms, but it cannot prove causation," she told Fox News Digital. "It does not demonstrate that weight-loss medications directly induce depression or suicidal thoughts."
The data was collected between 2013 and 2022.

"During most of this period, modern GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists used for weight loss (such as high-dose semaglutide/Wegovy or tirzepatide/Zepbound/Mounjaro) were either not yet on the market or had very limited real world uptake in South Korea," Mitchell said.
WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE
"The study sample captures older anti-obesity agents historically prescribed in South Korea during that decade, including phentermine, diethylpropion, phendimetrazine, topiramate and orlistat."
Central nervous system stimulants – including phentermine-based drugs – have been shown to carry risks of anxiety, mood changes and insomnia, the counselor noted.
Weight regain or perceived "failure" in weight management can trigger profound guilt, shame, helplessness and psychological distress, according to a mental health counselor. (iStock)
"The study highlighted a striking sub finding that found users who gained weight despite taking the medication had 4.2 times higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to non-users," Mitchell noted.
Weight regain or perceived "failure" in weight management can trigger profound guilt, shame, helplessness and psychological distress, according to the expert.

"Individuals with severe obesity have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia," Mitchell said. "A cross-sectional survey cannot separate pre-existing mental health struggles from new symptoms that arose after starting a medication."
"Any active suicidal thoughts require immediate emergency medical care."

More research is needed to determine whether weight-loss medications themselves affect mental health, or whether depression and other symptoms are related to factors such as obesity or difficulties losing weight.
The researchers also need to determine whether mental health risks differ between specific weight-loss drugs.
NEW WEIGHT-LOSS COMPOUND MELTS FAT WITHOUT CURBING APPETITE — AND PRESERVES MUSCLE

"Even though GLP-1 clinical trials show low absolute risk, the FDA’s product labels for chronic weight management drugs (like Wegovy and Zepbound) include warnings to monitor for mood changes," Mitchell noted.

She recommends that a physician conducts a baseline mental health history before prescribing new weight-loss medications, evaluating past or current depression, bipolar disorder, or history of suicidal ideation or behavior.

More research is needed to determine whether weight-loss medications themselves affect mental health, or whether depression and other symptoms are related to factors such as obesity or difficulties losing weight. (iStock)
"Individuals with severe obesity have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia."

"Doctors can inform patients and caregivers about potential mood changes so they know what to watch for," Mitchell said. "The next important step for ongoing monitoring would be to schedule check-ins at 4- to 8-week intervals during dose escalation, to evaluate both physiological progress and psychological well-being."

Patients should contact their healthcare provider immediately if they notice new or worsening depressive symptoms, including the following.

Persistent low mood, unexplained sadness or severe fatigueAnhedonia (loss of interest in activities once enjoyed)Increased anxiety, agitation, panic attacks or extreme restlessnessSleep disturbance or insomniaNew or worsening thoughts of self-harm or suicideMarked changes in behavior or personality, reported by friends or family

"Any active suicidal thoughts require immediate emergency medical care," Mitchell advised.
"If a patient develops emergent depression or suicidal ideation during treatment, clinicians should discontinue the weight-loss medication and connect the patient with psychiatric support."
Eli Lilly, manufacturer of the tirzepatide weight-loss medication Zepbound, explicitly mentions "depression or thoughts of suicide" in its safety information.

"You should pay attention to changes in your mood, behaviors, feelings or thoughts," the website reads.
It further advises patients to contact a healthcare provider if mental health changes are "new, worse or worry you."
An expert recommends that a physician conducts a baseline mental health history before prescribing new weight-loss medications. (iStock)
On Lilly's medical-information site, the company says that after reviewing clinical trials and medical reports, "no increased risk" of suicidal ideation or psychiatric adverse effects was identified.

Novo Nordisk, manufacturer of the semaglutide weight-loss medication Wegovy, states in its trials that less than 1% of participants experienced suicidal ideation or behavior during treatment. It also says there was "no difference between semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo."

title: Joe Biden shares health update after prostate cancer diagnosis while issuing warning to others
summary: Joe Biden revealed his radiation treatment from last fall "worked as intended" as he urged men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors.
story: Jill Biden admits former President Joe Biden experienced a decline in mental acuity, "slowing down" and "stuttering more" during his term due to exhaustion, despite her urging him to seek re-election. Rep. Claudia Tenney comments on the situation, suggesting it's an opportunity for Jill Biden to gain power, highlighting the former First Lady's own upcoming book.

Former President Joe Biden shared an update on his battle with prostate cancer Tuesday, revealing that radiation treatment he underwent last fall "worked as intended" while urging American men not to delay conversations with their doctors about cancer screening.
Biden, 83, issued the update in a lengthy social media post marking Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, saying the occasion was more personal for him following his diagnosis last year.
"The radiation treatment from last fall worked as intended, and I continue to do the things I care about, like finishing my memoir," Biden wrote.
JILL BIDEN SAYS FORMER PRESIDENT WILL LIVE WITH STAGE 4 CANCER 'FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE,' HAS SLOWED DOWN
President Joe Biden speaks at the White House in Washington, D.C. (Reuters)
He also thanked the doctors, nurses and other medical professionals who have treated him, saying their "skill, dedication, and compassion mean so much."
Biden used much of the message to urge men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors, pointing to the dramatically higher survival rate when the disease is detected early.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

Joe Biden continues radiation therapy for Stage 4 prostate cancer that has metastasized to bone, with aides saying the 83-year-old former president remains active and engaged. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Talk to your doctors. Ask the hard questions. Do it for yourself, and do it for the people who love you," Biden wrote.

Biden said men at average risk should begin discussing prostate cancer screening with their doctors around age 50, while Black men and those with a family history should begin those conversations earlier.
SIMPLE SITTING CHANGE LINKED TO LOWER RISK OF CANCER DEATH, STUDY FINDS

The American Cancer Society recommends discussing screening at age 50 for average-risk men, age 45 for Black men and certain men with a family history, and age 40 for some men at even higher risk. (iStock)
The American Cancer Society recommends discussing screening at age 50 for average-risk men, age 45 for Black men and certain men with a family history, and age 40 for some men at even higher risk.
Biden’s office announced in May 2025 that the former president had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had metastasized to his bones.
JOE BIDEN'S CANCER HAS SPREAD FURTHER, LEAVING HIM IN 'VERY PAINFUL' CONDITION, HUNTER REVEALS
Former President Joe Biden shared this picture of him and Jill Biden after it was announced he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. (X/JoeBiden)

The diagnosis came after Biden experienced increasing urinary symptoms and doctors discovered a prostate nodule. His office said at the time that the cancer had a Gleason score of 9, Grade Group 5, but was hormone-sensitive, allowing for effective management.
Biden later underwent radiation therapy and completed that course of treatment last fall.

Biden closed Tuesday's message by thanking those who have continued to pray for him and his family. (Grant Baldwin/Getty Images)

title: Drug developed for lung disease may slow biological aging in surprising ‘bonus’
summary: Rentosertib, an AI-discovered drug for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, made patients appear three to four years biologically younger in a clinical trial.
story: A drug being developed to treat a serious lung disease may also help to slow the aging process, first author Alex Zhavoronkov, PhD, founder and co-CEO of Insilico Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
A drug being developed to treat a serious lung disease may also help to slow the aging process, researchers say.
In a small clinical study, patients who took rentosertib – developed by Insilico Medicine in Massachusetts – showed changes in blood proteins that made them appear biologically younger.
Several tests estimated that after treatment, the patients were biologically about three to four years younger.
EATING COMMON DAIRY FOOD EVERY DAY MAY SLOW BIOLOGICAL AGING, STUDY SUGGESTS

"There is a promising trend in age reversal in addition to treating the disease, and it came as a bonus for disease treatment," first author Alex Zhavoronkov, PhD, founder and co-CEO of Insilico Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
A drug being developed to treat a serious lung disease may also help to slow the aging process, researchers say. (iStock)
"It basically means that you are predicted to be younger using a validated set of aging clocks. We don’t know what that means yet."
The results were published in Nature Biotechnology and presented Monday at the Nature conference at Sorbonne University in Paris.
ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION
The researchers caution, however, that this does not yet prove the drug can actually reverse aging or help people live longer.
"It’s early days," Zhavoronkov noted. "The drug is still investigational."
What is rentosertib?

Rentosertib is an experimental drug, discovered with the help of artificial intelligence, that is being developed to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a serious disease that causes scarring in the lungs.
In an unexpected outcome, the drug was found to change patterns of proteins in the blood in ways that made patients appear an average of three to four years younger, in one case up to six years.

Rentosertib is an experimental drug, discovered with the help of artificial intelligence, that is being developed to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a serious disease that causes scarring in the lungs. (iStock)
Six different aging tests showed the same general pattern, with patients who took rentosertib "scoring" biologically younger than those who received a placebo.
The strongest effect was seen after four weeks in patients taking 30 mg of the drug twice a day.
LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS

When researchers compared the results with data from more than 55,000 people in the UK Biobank, they found that the drug changed several blood proteins in the opposite direction from what is normally seen with aging.
The researchers also found signs that the drug may affect aging at the cellular level, as it changed processes involved in how cells function and respond to damage.
"Everybody agrees that living longer should be a fundamental human right for everyone."
Zhavoronkov said the company's approach uses AI to search for what he calls "molecular criminals" — biological targets that may contribute to both aging and disease.

The study – which was published in Nature Biotechnology – involved researchers from Insilico Medicine as well as Harvard Medical School, Stanford University, the Broad Institute, RWTH Aachen University, Peking University and Westlake University.
Study limitations
Zhavoronkov stressed that the findings are preliminary. "This is a pilot," he said. "It is early [and] exploratory."
The study had some limitations, including the small sample size – just 42 patients were analyzed over a 12-week period.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The participants all had IPF, which can change many of the same proteins researchers use to measure biological aging. This means it’s possible that the improvements in the participants’ lung disease was related to the changes in blood proteins.

Larger and longer trials – including healthy older adults and populations without IPF – are needed to determine whether the drug truly has anti-aging effects and whether they could lead to better health. (iStock)
The findings don’t prove that the drug actually slows aging, keeps people healthier longer or extends their lives, the researchers acknowledged.
The results were based only on changes in proteins in their blood, and do not yet support the use of rentosertib as an anti-aging treatment.
Risks and side effects
The risks and side effects associated with rentosertib were found to be "manageable," according to Dr. Carol Ann Satler, senior vice president of clinical development for Insilico Medicine.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The most common potential side effects included mild diarrhea, slightly lower potassium levels in the blood and temporary increases in liver enzymes.
The drug was found to change patterns of proteins in the blood in ways that made patients appear an average of three to four years younger, in one case up to six years. (Insilico Medicine)
"Once you stop the drug, essentially, they return to normal," Satler told Fox News Digital.
In the next trial, the doctor said, "We'll be looking to adjust the doses of the drug based on the side effect profile so that people can stay on it longer."
Looking ahead
Rentosertib has now progressed into a year-long phase 3 study of more than 300 patients in China, according to Insilico.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Larger and longer trials – including healthy older adults and populations without IPF – are needed to determine whether the drug truly has anti-aging effects and whether they could lead to better health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While more research lies ahead, Zhavoronkov said the findings have given him more confidence to continue pursuing drugs that could target both age-related diseases and aging itself.
"Everybody agrees that living longer should be a fundamental human right for everyone," he said.

story: Dr. Annu Navani, chief medical officer at Le Reve Wellness, revelas why people should focus on adding healthy years to life — not chasing immortality.
A Texas woman who just turned 105 attributes her long life to "the good Lord."
While Blynda Vidock's faith may have played an important role in her longevity, the Baytown resident has also followed many of the habits that experts say can contribute to a longer, healthier life.

"The good Lord put me here for so many years, and it’s His life through me," she told FOX 26 Houston at her recent birthday celebration. "But I’ve always been very athletic, played tennis, swam all my life and ate good food."
GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE
Vidock joked that she preaches to her children, grandchildren and "great-grands" to eat healthier, but said, "They still eat junk food!"
"We live faster nowadays," she said. "We used to have time to sit down and have a meal together."
Blynda Vidock celebrated more than a century of life with loved ones, joking at her birthday gathering that she had been made "queen for a day." (FOX 26 Houston KRIV)

Vidock was born in 1921 and grew up in West Palm Beach, Florida. While working for $15 a week at a bank in West Palm Beach, she crossed paths with big-name movie stars Clark Gable and Fred Astaire, and also recalled encountering a young John F. Kennedy.
She met Coast Guardsman Charles "Chuck" Vidock while volunteering with the USO during World War II. The two married and moved to Texas in 1946 and spent decades traveling the world together.
LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS
Vidock is "completely sharp, independent and full of stories from a century of living," according to the report.
A video from her birthday party shows the centenarian walking around and chatting animatedly with the many friends and family members who gathered to honor her.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"It’s wonderful to have you people here, and I don’t know if I’m supposed to dance or sing or get up on the table," she said. "I think I've been made queen for a day, and I've got my 15 minutes of fame, so you better enjoy it because it won't come again."
Every morning when she wakes up, Vidock said she wonders, "‘This is another day, Lord, why am I here?’" adding, "Every day is a blessing!"
Blynda Vidock celebrated her 105th birthday surrounded by friends and family in Texas. (FOX 26 Houston KRIV)
She said "the saddest part about getting old" is watching people lose their mental sharpness and credits "the good Lord" with allowing her to keep hers.
Vidock said a few simple habits have helped her live so long.
