title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announces distribution of more than 7 million free eggs statewide
summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced 1.7 million free eggs have reached Texas food banks, with 5.3 million more on the way from a settlement.
story: FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble reports from Matteson, IL, highlighting the struggle of local egg farmers like Marty Thomas. Despite surging egg supply driving consumer prices down, farmers face losses as their production costs remain high, forcing them to adapt.

More than 1.7 million free eggs have already been delivered to Texas food banks, with another 5.3 million slated to arrive in the coming weeks as part of an antitrust settlement with three major egg producers, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday.

The statewide distribution stems from settlements reached in June with Cal-Maine Foods, Centrum/Versova and Hickman's Egg Ranch, resolving antitrust claims brought by the Trump administration's Department of Justice and a coalition of state attorneys general over allegations the companies conspired to inflate egg prices between 2022 and 2025.
Under the agreements, the companies will donate more than 7 million eggs to Texas food banks and pay a combined $3.3 million to participating states.

"After securing 7 million eggs for the people of Texas, I am excited to announce that Texans will now have an opportunity to receive cartons of free eggs in communities across the state," Paxton said. "I will continue to help our families put food on the table and do everything within my power to lower prices and help Texans who are struggling to make ends meet."
TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO

Ken Paxton announced that more than 7 million free eggs will be distributed to Texas food banks under antitrust settlements with three major egg producers. (Antranik Tavitian/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The distributions are being coordinated with Feeding Texas, the state's largest hunger-relief organization. Seventeen food banks are participating in the effort.

The Houston Food Bank is expected to receive the largest allocation with 1,544,400 eggs, followed by the North Texas Food Bank in Plano and the Tarrant Area Food Bank in Fort Worth, which will each receive 842,400 eggs. Other participating food banks are located across the state, including Austin, San Antonio, Tyler, Corpus Christi, El Paso, Laredo, Odessa, Pharr, Beaumont, Amarillo, Lubbock, Victoria, Abilene and Wichita Falls.
AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE
A man reaches for food supplies at a pantry serving families in need. (Olivianna Calmes)
It was not immediately clear when individual food banks would begin distributing the eggs to Texans or whether eligibility requirements would vary by location.

Cartons of eggs are stacked in a packing facility. Texas officials say more than 7 million eggs will be distributed to food banks statewide through an antitrust settlement with three major egg producers. (Matthias Bein/picture alliance via Getty Images)

A spokesperson for Feeding Texas did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on distribution timing and how Texans can receive the eggs. Fox News Digital also reached out to Cal-Maine Foods for comment on the settlement and the statewide donation effort.

title: Local GOP leader slams $50K taxpayer 'slush fund' for families of detained, deported immigrant breadwinners
summary: A Virginia GOP leader calls Arlington County's $50,000 in taxpayer-funded grants for families of deported illegal immigrants a "slush fund."
story: Leaders in a Virginia county recently approved a measure to pay families up to $2,000 if the primary wage earner is detained or removed by immigration authorities.

A Virginia GOP leader is pushing back against a new county program to provide taxpayer-funded grants to the families of illegal immigrants whose primary wage earner was detained or deported by federal immigration authorities.
Arlington County, which sits across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., endorsed a plan on Sept. 2 to appropriate $50,000 for the social safety net program.
Under the terms of the project, the funds would be given to the nonprofit Arlington Thrive, which would provide up to $2,000 to the families to cover basic needs.

"This flies in the face of the Trump administration policy, and it is a detriment to taxpayers of Arlington, tens of thousands of whom are conservative and Republican and oppose this policy," Matthew Hurtt, chairman of the Arlington County GOP, told Fox News Digital.
'ALIEN HARBORING' ACCUSATIONS FLY AS DC-AREA COUNTY SPENDS TAXPAYER FUNDS TO BLUNT ICE

Federal immigration authorities make an arrest in Arlington, Va., in February. Arlington County leaders recently voted to set aside $50,000 to give families up to $2,000 if the primary wage earner was detained by immigration authorities. (ICE)

Hurtt described the money as a "slush fund" designed to further oppose the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. He noted that since Arlington Thrive is a nonprofit, it is exempt from transparency protocols that normally apply to government agencies.
The County Board praised the program at a special meeting, where it voted 4-0 with one member absent.
FIRST ON FOX: ICE QUIETLY ARRESTS JAW-DROPPING NUMBER OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IN MASSIVE DC AREA OPERATION
Arlington County GOP Chair Matthew Hurtt sounded off on his home county's "slush fund" for the families of migrants detained or deported by federal authorities. (Arlington County)
"We stand with our immigrant families, and we will not stop doing so," Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said. "We are valuing the families of those that have been displaced and removed."
The move follows a recent law enforcement operation in which more than 1,300 illegal immigrants were arrested over a two-week period in the Washington, D.C., and Virginia area.
DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST
In January, as part of the county's opposition to immigration enforcement, de Ferranti urged residents to report sightings of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to county authorities.

Arlington County, as well as other counties in Northern Virginia, have for years tried to subvert the Trump administration's efforts to fight illegal immigration through various sanctuary policies, Hurtt said.
DOJ ACCUSES MARYLAND OF 'ACTIVE AND DELIBERATE EFFORT' TO PREVENT DEPORTATIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: LAWSUIT
"Arlington County, Fairfax County, and other Northern Virginia counties are completely run by far-left activists who love this kind of program," Hurtt said. (Universal Images Group/Getty Images)

"Arlington County, Fairfax County and other Northern Virginia counties are completely run by far-left activists who love this kind of program," he said. "They have, for years, since President Trump's first administration, sought to be the first line of defense against the orange man.
"So, if something happens in Washington that is supported by Republicans, the county board in Arlington and Fairfax does exactly the opposite."
Meanwhile, Hurtt said, county leaders have pushed for voters to support bond measures for critical services, which are covered by additional taxes.
Hurtt accused Arlington County of "prioritizing these far-left projects like a slush fund for illegal aliens." (Courtesy of the Department of Homeland Security)

"Every single election cycle, the Arlington County board puts hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballot in the form of bond issues for basic services — school improvements, road construction and other projects that they deem necessary," he said.

"What that tells voters is that they aren't prioritizing those projects, projects that they bond out and borrow dollar after dollar, but they're prioritizing these far-left projects like a slush fund for illegal aliens."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Arlington County Democrats and the County Board for comment.

title: Top Republican names who he says is really leading Democrats — and it's not Schumer or Jeffries
summary: Top Senate Republican Rick Scott claims Chuck Schumer isn't leading Democrats — saying AOC, Zohran Mamdani and Hassan Piker call the shots.
story: Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., warned that it's not really Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer nor House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries running the show, it's Hassan Piker, AOC and far-left progressives.
DALLAS — A top Senate Republican warned that the real leaders of the Democratic Party aren’t the top two Democrats in Congress.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., weren’t the ones calling the shots for Democrats — it’s the far-left progressives, both inside and out of Congress, that are leading the way.
"Let's be clear, the leader of the Democrat Party is not Schumer, it's not Jeffries," Scott said. "It's Hasan Piker, it is AOC and [Zohran] Mamdani."
REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Hasan Piker, (Sarah Rice/Getty Images; Florencia Tan Jun/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

Republicans are congregating in Dallas, Texas, to pitch why they should maintain power in Congress and energize their base during a midterm cycle in which Democrats are fighting to retake control of both chambers.

Scott, who once led the Senate GOP’s campaign arm known as the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), argued that Schumer and Senate Democrats could "salivate all they want, but their message is horrible."

That message is driven by the likes of streamer Hasan Piker, who has come under fire from both Republicans and Democrats, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION
"They're going to say, ‘Gosh, we want men to play in women's sports, to destroy women's sport,’" Scott said. "They can talk about socialism, how they want to kill all the capitalists."

"I tell people, you go vote for a Democrat, which is now a socialist, right? Then you better buy a bunch of guns," he continued. "Because you can vote socialism in, ask the people in Venezuela, but guess what? You can't get rid of it without guns."

Still, Republicans are facing political headwinds as November creeps closer, with the Iran war still raging, prices at the gas pump and checkout line still high, and a fresh trade war with Canada putting GOP incumbents and candidates in a bind.
'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN
Sen. Rick Scott in the Senate Subway during a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 14, 2025. (Allison Robbert/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

And midterm elections are more often than not a referendum against the party in power. Scott, however, believes that Republicans are going to "actually have a good cycle," and maintain control of the Senate.

"The reason is we have a better message and we have great candidates," Scott said. "If you look at our Senate candidates, I mean, how would you like to be out and defend [Abdul] El-Sayed's record of being antisemitic and hating this country."
Much of the purpose of the convention, Scott acknowledged, was to remind voters that while his name isn’t explicitly on the ballot, the midterm elections were all about President Donald Trump.

Trump is set to speak on Wednesday night as the NFL starts again, and as Republicans formulate their final message to their base. And that message is that if Democrats win, Trump’s agenda will stall completely.
"There's no question the Trump agenda is on the ballot," Scott said. "If you want the Trump agenda accomplished, we have to control the House, we have to control the Senate."
"And if the Democrats control the House, they're gonna impeach him for combing his hair the wrong way," he continued. "So we've gotta control the House and we gotta control the Senate."

title: Florida sues Netflix, alleges streamer tracked children after promising families privacy
summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier alleges Netflix secretly harvested children's behavioral data to build the ad business it vowed never to create.
story: Fox News correspondent Madeleine Rivera reports on Netflix countering a Texas lawsuit that accuses it of privacy violations and using addictive design to target children on ‘Fox Report.’

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued Netflix on Wednesday, accusing the streaming giant of misleading subscribers by promising an ad-free, privacy-focused service while secretly collecting years of behavioral data — including from children's profiles — to build the advertising business it long insisted it would never create.

The 66-page lawsuit alleges Netflix built its brand by assuring consumers that paying a monthly subscription meant they could avoid the surveillance-driven advertising model used by other major technology companies. Instead, Florida alleges Netflix quietly collected extensive user data before launching its ad-supported platform in November 2022.

"Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape Big Tech surveillance. That was false," Uthmeier said in a news release announcing the lawsuit. "Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build. Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable."

The complaint points to repeated public statements from Netflix executives who touted the company as different from advertising-supported competitors. Among them, the lawsuit cites former CEO Reed Hastings, who said during a 2020 earnings call that Netflix was "not integrating everybody's data," adding, "We don't collect anything," and describing the streaming service as "the safe respite" from companies that exploit users through advertising.
WASHINGTON POST FACES CLASS-ACTION LAWSUIT ALLEGING 'SURVEILLANCE PRICING' OF SUBSCRIBERS
The Netflix logo is shown on one of their buildings in the Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles on Dec. 2, 2025. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

Florida alleges those assurances were misleading because Netflix built what the lawsuit describes as a massive behavioral-data operation that records how subscribers use the platform. According to the complaint, Netflix tracks billions of user interactions, including what subscribers watch, search for, pause, rewind, skip and abandon, along with information about their devices and locations. The state alleges Netflix uses that information to improve its recommendation systems and support its advertising business.

The lawsuit places particular emphasis on Netflix's Kids Profiles, which the company markets as dedicated spaces designed for children. Florida alleges Netflix encouraged parents to create children's profiles by describing them as "Great for kids" and a child's "own space" while continuing to collect and analyze children's viewing behavior through the same telemetry systems used for adult accounts.
PARENTS PUSH CONGRESS TO ACT ON KIDS' ONLINE SAFETY AFTER JURIES FIND META AND YOUTUBE LIABLE FOR HARM

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced a lawsuit accusing Netflix of misleading subscribers about its data collection practices and children's privacy. (Amy Beth Bennett/South Florida Sun Sentinel)

Florida also accuses Netflix of using so-called "dark patterns" to keep viewers engaged. The complaint alleges autoplay, which is enabled by default on Kids Profiles, is intentionally designed to extend viewing sessions, increase binge watching and generate additional behavioral data, particularly from children.

The state further alleges Netflix expanded into the advertising business it once rejected by allowing advertisers and advertising technology companies to use subscriber data for audience targeting and campaign measurement after launching its ad-supported tier in November 2022.

The lawsuit accuses Netflix of violating the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and the Florida Digital Bill of Rights. Among other claims, Florida alleges Netflix unlawfully shared sensitive personal data collected from children without obtaining the consent required under state law.
MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES
In this photo illustration, the logos of media service providers, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ and Hulu are displayed on the screen of an Apple MacBook Pro screen. (Chesnot)

Uthmeier is asking the court to permanently block the alleged practices, order Netflix to delete data the state says was deceptively collected from Floridians, stop using historical subscriber data to support its advertising business, purge behavioral data collected through Kids Profiles, prohibit the use of alleged dark-pattern designs and impose civil penalties authorized under Florida law.

Netflix did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Radical leftist podcaster viciously attacks Melania Trump in graphic curse-laden rant
summary: Podcaster Jennifer Welch called first lady Melania Trump "an absolutely horrific person" in a profanity-laden rant targeting the Trump family.
story: Far-left podcaster Jennifer Welch incites a heated debate by attacking homeschooling parents on her YouTube show, 'I've Had It.' Welch controversially describes homeschooling as 'trickle-down stupidity,' 'MAGA on steroids,' and MAHA. She claims 'America has a crazy Christian problem,' leading Tomi Lahren and Brian Kilmeade to critique her divisive statements and popularity.
A far-left podcaster known for her vile, often curse-laden rants against the political right took aim at first lady Melania Trump in a recent episode of her show.
"I don't like anything for Melania," Jennifer Welch said in a clip making its rounds on social media.
"And I wish I could be the bigger person and say that I do, but I don't," she continued. "I don't like anything possible for her. She is, I think, just an absolutely horrific person."
MELANIA TRUMP CALLS FOR ABC TO FIRE JIMMY KIMMEL OVER ‘HATEFUL AND VIOLENT RHETORIC'
Far-left podcast star Jennifer Welch has emerged as a darling of the liberal media. (Bryan Bedder/Getty Images for GLAAD)
Other recent clips attacking homeschool parents and late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham have earned Welch a description as a member of the "dirtbag left."
She describes herself as an "atheist from the Bible Belt" and often levies attacks against Christianity.

Welch, after calling the first lady "horrific" in her recent podcast episode, launched into a rant about a controversy involving a model and former diplomat, who was a friend of Melania's, threatening in April to expose unspecified information about the first lady and President Donald Trump.
Then, the left-wing podcaster turned to taking a dig at the first couple's sex lives.

"She cared enough in the bogus $40 million payoff she got to make sure that everybody — not only in the United States, but in the world — knows she does not screw her husband," Welch said, referring to Amazon's $40 million purchase of the rights to the "Melania" documentary.
Melania Trump at the red carpet at the "Melania" premiere. (Nikos DeGruccio/Fox News Digital)
There are no details about intimacy between the pair in the movie, according to a transcript of the film.
Still, Welch persisted.
KIMMEL CALLS MELANIA TRUMP AN ‘EXPECTANT WIDOW’ BEFORE WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER SHOOTING

"They could have cut that part out, but she made sure the world knows, 'I do not screw my husband.' So I'm not buying into this that Melania all of the sudden is liberated and doesn't give a s--- about stuff anymore, because I think that's the thing that eats the Trumps up all the time.
"They care what everybody thinks about them, and they want to change everybody's opinion on them."
The first lady's office did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment on the podcaster's remarks.
President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump attend a 9/11 observance event in the courtyard of the Pentagon Sept. 11, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Welsh also attacked the rest of the Trumps in the episode, saying that even if they received the highest praise, the family members would still be "broken."

"We are elevating the bad guy right here," Welsh said. "We are elevating the most dysfunctional family in the United States, and wrapping it up in traditional Christian values. It’s just such bulls---."

Welch makes a habit on her podcast of discussing the private lives of Republicans. When Sen. Graham died, she graphically discussed long-circulated rumors that he was gay.

title: Rubio designates Ecuadorian gang linked to drug trafficking a terrorist group
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the designation during a visit to Quito, accusing Los Tiguerones of aiding cartels and attacking civilians, police and journalists.
story: Armed gunmen infiltrated the studio of TC Television in Guayaquil, Ecuador, Tuesday. Courtesy: Reuters
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said he has designated a new Ecuador-based gang as a foreign terrorist organization and specially designated global terrorist.
Los Tiguerones, which has been linked to narcotrafficking and other illicit activity, has been accused of funding criminal activity against law enforcement and civilians.

"Los Tiguerones is yet another Ecuadorian gang helping Mexican cartels move and export illicit drugs to fund terrorism and criminal activity including attacks against civilians, law enforcement, and journalists," Rubio said in a post on X.
Rubio added that the group was also behind the notorious 2024 attack on an Ecuadorian television station, when armed men stormed the studio and took staff hostage during a live broadcast.
ARMED GUNMEN TAKE OVER ECUADOR TV STUDIO DURING LIVE BROADCAST, THREATEN STAFF: 'A TERRORIST ACT'

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a news conference after meeting with the Ecuadorian Foreign Minister Roberto Kury and other officials at the US Embassy in Quito, Ecuador, Wednesday. (Pool/Fox News)

During the raid, attackers forced staff to the floor at gunpoint and allegedly stuffed a stick of dynamite into an employee’s pocket, according to The Associated Press (AP). The assault unfolded on live television for 15 minutes before the feed was cut, the AP reported. At least 13 suspects were reportedly arrested after police regained control of the building.
Rubio said Wednesday’s decision comes on the heels of the designation of three other groups, including Los Lobos and Los Choneros, in July.
"They're not ordinary. These are violent, bloodthirsty terrorist organizations. And we have to make sure that we continue to pursue them," Rubio said.
The announcement was made while Rubio was visiting Quito, Ecuador, as part of a three-nation tour to strengthen economic and security ties with Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.
FILE — Rubio said Los Tiguerones were responsible for taking over a live broadcast at TC Television in Guayaquil, Ecuador. (TC Television network via AP)
TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

During a press conference, Rubio said the U.S. will also target corrupt officials accused of collaborating with terrorists as part of efforts to dismantle the organizations."We'll be announcing the designation of seven former members of the government here, officials for accepting bribes and for betraying their most essential duties," he said.
The designation will cut such terrorist groups off from U.S. financial assets, property and other resources that could be used to carry out attacks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio (L) speaks as Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ecuador Roberto Kury listens during a conference as part of an official visit to Ecuador at Carondelet Palace on Sept. 9, 2026, in Quito, Ecuador. (Franklin Jacome/Agencia Press South/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rubio said the U.S. "will never stop fighting against the violent narcoterrorists who flood our nation with deadly drugs."

"Today’s action taken by the State Department further demonstrates that the Trump Administration continues to deliver on its promises to the American people to dismantle cartels and narcoterrorist networks in our region, ensuring the safety of the American people," he added.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Emergency slide sparks questions on Trump’s new Air Force One before president reveals why
summary: An emergency slide deployed from the Qatar-gifted Boeing 747 at Joint Base Andrews before Trump explained it was part of a routine safety check.
story: President Donald Trump comments on the inspection of an emergency slide aboard Air Force One after arriving at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on ‘America Reports.’
An emergency slide deployment on the Qatari-gifted Air Force One raised questions at Joint Base Andrews (JBA) on Wednesday before President Donald Trump revealed it was all part of a safety check.

"They were checking it before, and they just wanted to make sure," Trump told reporters on the tarmac after exiting Marine One. "So they’ve, I guess, already put it up. They want to make sure everything works perfectly."
A person briefed on the situation told Fox News that military personnel had accidentally triggered the slide.
White House communications director Steven Cheung confirmed the plane was cleared for the president’s trip.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SUBPOENAS NY TIMES JOURNALISTS IN GRAND JURY LEAK PROBE TIED TO AIR FORCE ONE REPORT

The emergency slide of Air Force One is deployed Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland ahead of President Donald Trump's trip to the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

"As the President has said, the slide was checked out to make sure everything works perfectly," Cheung told Fox News. "Air Force One is on its way to Dallas so he can deliver his much-anticipated speech to a raucous and sold-out crowd."
The unusual scene unfolded after Marine One rolled to a stop near the presidential aircraft, with Trump remaining aboard the helicopter, and the slide could be seen extending from the plane.
The White House print pool reported spotting what appeared to be an inflatable emergency slide deployed from the right side front door of the Qatari-gifted Boeing 747.
The door is opposite the entrance Trump typically uses to board the plane.

At the same time, the older white-and-blue Air Force One was seen moving out of its hangar and into position a few hundred yards behind the newer aircraft. The older jet then deployed its front and rear stairs.
TRUMP EXPLAINS WHY HE'S FLYING OLD AIR FORCE ONE BACK TO DC
The door of Marine One remained closed as of 2:19 p.m., according to the pool, fueling questions about whether the unexpected slide deployment had disrupted the president’s travel plans.
Trump later emerged from the helicopter and said the equipment had been tested to ensure it was working properly, indicating there had not been an emergency aboard the aircraft.

President Donald Trump boards Air Force One as crew members work on an emergency slide that inflated off the side of the plane Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Asked whether he was confident the plane was safe to fly, Trump responded, "I am. I am. Or I wouldn’t be on it."

It was not immediately clear whether the safety check would affect which plane Trump would use for his next flight.
Fox News' Nick Rojas contributed to this report.

title: 'Alien harboring' accusations fly as DC-area county spends taxpayer funds to blunt ICE
summary: A Virginia county faces fire for a new policy providing taxpayer-funded grants to families of illegal immigrants whose breadwinner was deported by ICE.
story: Former Acting DHS Secretary Chad Wolf discusses Fairfax County, Va., handing illegal immigrant alleged sex predator Israel Flores-Ortiz over to I.C.E. on 'America Reports.'
FIRST ON FOX: A Virginia county is under fire for a new policy providing taxpayer funds in the form of grants to families of illegal immigrants whose breadwinner was detained or deported by ICE.

Arlington County, which sits just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., is not new to policies critics say interfere with DHS operations, as it previously caused outrage when the chair of the Arlington County board publicly suggested residents call police to report ICE sightings in January.

"If you look at the alien harboring statute – do you do anything to encourage or induce people to either come illegally or that are illegally here to stay, that could be arguably a violation of the alien harboring statute?" former acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey told Fox News Digital in a Wednesday interview.
DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS
Arlington County Board of Supervisors, from left, Julius D. "JD" Spain Sr., Susan Cunningham, Takis Karantonis, Board Chair Matt de Ferranti and Vice Chair Maureen Coffey. (Arlington County)
"By giving money to people… the reasonable inference is that these people are also illegal, the money enables them to stay in the country illegally, because they lost their breadwinner," Fahey said.

He said Arlington County Manager Mark Schwartz’s comments to ARLNow that many of the affected families are "unbanked" – or lack access to financial institutions which statutorily require identification to open deposit accounts – is itself a tell.
TAXPAYER-FUNDED HOUSING FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IN GOP'S CROSSHAIRS: 'IT'S GOT TO STOP'
Illegal immigrants are arrested by ICE officers in the D.C. area. (Courtesy of the Department of Homeland Security)

"That shows the county knows the money is going to be going to people that are illegally here and it will help them stay. So that's where I think the alien harboring statute comes into play," he said, adding the county shows "reckless disregard" for the fact their policies accommodate people in the country illegally.

Arlington will start by setting aside $50,000 to be distributed through "social safety-net" ministry ArlingtonThrive in increments of up to $2,000 per affected family to cover basic needs and utilities, according to reports.

The plan – which passed 4-0 with one board member absent – reportedly formed after a major ICE operation in Maryland and Virginia netted 1,328 illegal immigrant arrests, including the case of a man who ran from agents when confronted near the U.S. Air Force Memorial.

Five regional federal Democrats sounded off afterward, endorsing an ensuing Arlington County Police investigation into the encounter between ICE and Jose Mejia Hernandez, who was reportedly tased and suffered a brain bleed.
Fox News Digital reached out to Arlington County officials, including Chairman Matt de Ferranti, a Democrat from Rock Spring.
"We are valuing the families of those that have been displaced and removed," he told local press.

In January, de Ferranti warned Arlingtonians that county law prohibits its "public safety professionals" from "interfering with enforcement of federal immigration law," but that his suggestion to call 911 to report ICE sightings helps officials know agents are present and pivot to "pursu[ing] Arlington County’s law enforcement mission: preventing violence in our community."
DOJ ACCUSES MARYLAND OF 'ACTIVE AND DELIBERATE EFFORT' TO PREVENT DEPORTATIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: LAWSUIT
Federal immigration authorities make an arrest in Arlington, Va., in February. (ICE)
Reckless disregard and inducement are both subsections of the law Fahey referenced – 8 U.S.C. 1324.
Leadership at the Department of Homeland Security was similarly critical of Arlington’s move.
"You can’t make this up," an agency spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
"Sanctuary politicians are taking Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars to reward illegal aliens who break the law. This insanity shows once again who they put first."

Fahey said counties cannot make their own immigration laws, and with Arlington in particular, their alleged "inducement" doesn’t just affect their county, as creating safe harbor for illegal immigrants can have ripple effects in adjacent areas like the District of Columbia, cities of Falls Church and Alexandria and Fairfax County.

"A person could go on and commit another crime somewhere outside of Arlington… you can’t have localities and states carving out their own immigration laws or saying immigration laws can’t be enforced [here]."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
A welcome sign is posted near the Key Bridge in Rosslyn, Arlington County, Virginia. (Universal Images Group/Getty Images)

Arguments against mass deportation on the grounds of family separation are similarly flawed, the former director said, pointing to the fact that when an American citizen is arrested or jailed, they are also physically "separated" from their family.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Latest dispatch from the People’s Republic of Arlington," read a critical posting on X.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Missouri Supreme Court threatens secretary of state with contempt amid intensifying redistricting battle
summary: Secretary of State Denny Hoskins must appear Thursday to explain why he shouldn't be held in contempt over Missouri's congressional maps battle.
story: Fox News correspondent Mark Meredith has the latest on the key storylines shaping the race to the 2026 midterm elections, including the political fallout from the Supreme Court's Missouri redistricting decision, the battle for control of Congress, and the issues driving voters as both parties intensify their push toward November on 'Special Report.'
The Missouri Supreme Court signaled Tuesday that it was considering holding Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt amid an escalating battle over proposed congressional maps.

Hoskins, a Republican, said Tuesday that he would keep using the congressional districts redrawn last year, despite a U.S. Supreme Court decision that left standing a state Supreme Court order requiring Missouri to use its old districts instead.
"I look forward to my day in court," Hoskins said in a post on X that cited the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution.
MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP

Missouri's high court blocked the new redistricting map and ordered a statewide vote in November on whether to keep it, amid efforts led by Republicans to redraw the state's congressional map. (AP Photo/David A. Lieb)
Hoskins must appear in court Thursday to explain why he shouldn't be held in contempt for instructing election officials to use the 2025 congressional map despite an injunction barring its use.
Last week, Missouri's high court ruled that the map backed by President Donald Trump cannot be used because thousands of voters signed a petition demanding a statewide referendum on it.
SUPREME COURT DEALS BLOW TO VIRGINIA DEMOCRATS IN FIGHT OVER STATE COURT ELECTION MAP RULING
Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to grant an emergency stay requested by Hoskins, leaving in place the injunction ordered by the state Supreme Court.

However, shortly after Kavanaugh's announcement, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, issued a temporary restraining order prohibiting Missouri from using any map other than the new 2025 districts.
GEORGIA REDISTRICTING BATTLE REVIVED AFTER APPEALS COURT OVERTURNS FEDERAL COURT DECISION
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway asked the U.S. Supreme Court to halt the state high court's decision immediately. (AP Photo/David A. Lieb)
Opponents of the new redistricting plan quickly filed a notice to appeal Clark's order to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
"An individual federal judge cannot overrule the Missouri Supreme Court," said attorney Chuck Hatfield, who represents People Not Politicians, the group that sponsored the referendum petition.
RNC AND NRCC FILE LAWSUIT DEFENDING MISSOURI'S NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP AGAINST DEMOCRATIC CHALLENGES
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said she was prepared to comply with Clark's order, which she argued "binds the state to using" the new congressional districts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We maintain that changing the congressional map in between the primary and general elections is simply not feasible and profoundly unjust to Missouri voters," she wrote on X.
BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES
The conflict is part of a broader, nationwide effort by Republicans to redraw congressional districts mid-decade to gain U.S. House seats.
Missouri currently has six Republicans and two Democrats in the U.S. House. The new redistricting plan would eliminate one Democratic seat, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Bipartisan duo launches congressional caucus to confront antisemitism at colleges
summary: GOP Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York and Democratic Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey are launching the Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus.
story: Representative Josh Gottheimer joins to discuss the growing divide within the Democratic Party over far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. As Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed distances himself from Piker, Gottheimer and other prominent Democrats condemn the streamer's controversial remarks.
Reps. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y. and Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., are launching a congressional coalition to target antisemitism at institutions of higher education.

The Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus will provide a bipartisan avenue for lawmakers to "coordinate oversight of how" schools of higher learning react to antisemitism, according to press releases issued by the lawmakers' offices.

The caucus will "press institutions to protect Jewish students, faculty, and staff, and to enforce their own anti-harassment and anti-discrimination policies," "advance and track federal legislation targeting campus antisemitism and BDS-driven discrimination," and "spotlight schools that are getting it right and share best practices across campuses nationwide," the releases note.
CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS
Rep. Elise Stefanik and Rep. Josh Gottheimer. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
While Gottheimer is a Jewish Democrat and Stefanik is a Catholic Republican, both lawmakers are concerned about the problem of antisemitism.

"Since October 7th, Jewish students on too many campuses have been harassed, intimidated, and made to feel like strangers in their own school," Gottheimer said, referring to the 2023 attack by Hamas terrorists in Israel.
TRUMP INDICATES SUPPORT FOR CHRISTIAN-BACKED PLAN TO HELP CANADIAN JEWS ESCAPE ANTISEMITISM
Rep. Elise Stefanik speaks at Faith and Freedom Coalitionâs Road to Majority Conference in Washington, D.C., on June 26, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"That’s why Elise and I are teaming up to launch this caucus to hold universities accountable, back up the schools getting it right, like Vanderbilt, and make sure every Jewish kid can have a college experience without fear of discrimination or violence," he noted.
Stefanik, the author of the book "Poisoned Ivies," noted that she has "been proud to be the leader in Congress on combatting antisemitism and anti-Americanism at our colleges and universities."
PIERS MORGAN EVISCERATES IVY LEAGUE STUDENT WHO REFUSED TO WORK 'FOR A JEW' AS 'BRAZENLY' ANTISEMITIC
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Gottheimer "has been a leading partner and legislator with whom I have worked on this critical issue," Stefanik noted. "We are committed to saving American higher education for the next generation."
Fox News' Kelly Phares contributed to this report.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Proposal would pay homeowners 'data center dividends' to counter growing backlash
summary: Think tank proposes sharing data center tax revenue with local residents through direct payments, tax credits or scholarships
story: Sam Lyman, head of research at the Bitcoin Policy Institute, tells Fox News Digital that AI communities are sitting on a digital goldmine and should share directly in the economic gains generated by data centers. "It can't just be the developers in Silicon Valley who are becoming wealthy from this revolution," he says.

As opposition to artificial intelligence data centers spreads across rural America, one group is proposing "data center dividends" to counter the backlash by allowing residents to share directly in the wealth generated by the technology hubs.

A new report from the Bitcoin Policy Institute, a think tank based in Washington, D.C., proposes that data center dividends are a model that would return part of the property tax revenue generated by AI data centers directly to households living in the communities that host the data centers, potentially providing annual payments of between about $4,500 and $8,900 per household without creating new taxes or increasing costs for developers.

"Every American deserves to benefit from the AI boom," Sam Lyman, head of research at the nonprofit, told Fox News Digital. "It can't just be the developers in Silicon Valley who are becoming wealthy from this revolution. It needs to be the Americans who are building the county infrastructure that makes these data centers possible in the first place."

The proposal comes as opposition to data centers intensifies nationwide, fomented over the past year by a network of socialists and communist nonprofits funded by a tech tycoon, Neville Roy Singham, living in Shanghai, supporting the Chinese Communist Party and a "new world order" promulgated by Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The opposition has widened to conservatives and centrists, with the report noting that Americans are now more likely to oppose a data center in their community than a nuclear power plant.

In a poll earlier this year, Gallup found that 71% of Americans oppose construction of an AI data center in their area, while only 53% oppose a nearby nuclear plant. The report says local data center moratoriums have exploded from six in 2024 to 59 last year and 294 last month.

Over the past year, groups in the Singham network – including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, the People's Forum, CodePink and BreakThrough News – have opposed data centers and also Flock surveillance cameras with aggressive media campaigns, elevating China as a technological powerhouse and denigrating any developments by U.S. technology companies.

"These influence actions are cognitive warfare. Foreign actors don't need Americans to become pro-China," Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity at the National Security Agency, recently told Fox News Digital. "They need Americans to argue for the outcomes Beijing wants. And a free society that can't build the power and govern the advanced technology is going to wind up renting it from the adversary, read the PRC, that doesn't share its own values. And that scares me as an American."

Sen Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez hold a press conference to announce the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act at the U.S. Capitol on March 25, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

Lyman said the political problem is that many Americans believe technology companies are reaping the benefits of the AI boom while local communities bear the costs. The propaganda campaigns by the pro-China groups are promoting that message by describing tech executives as "oligarchs" and "imperialists." One constant message in the campaigns is "People Over Profits."

"I really think that data center dividends will reverse the momentum in the data center debate, because suddenly every American who lives in these counties where data centers might be built recognizes that he or she can have a material stake in the AI economy," said Lyman, a former senior advisor and speechwriter for Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Protesters react as the Box Elder County Commission approves a large AI data center project in Tremonton, Utah, on May 4, 2026. Activists opposed the 40,000-acre development over concerns about water use, energy demand and environmental impact. (Natalie Behring/Getty Images)

Polling cited in the report found that 73% of Americans believe the costs of data center construction outweigh the benefits, while voters overwhelmingly believe AI will primarily enrich executives and business owners rather than workers.

Rather than creating a new tax, the proposal would redirect a portion of property tax revenue that counties already collect from data centers. "Data center dividends can ensure that rural Americans rise in the age of AI alongside the engineers developing this technology," the report notes.
An Amazon Web Services data center in Aldie, Virginia, on May 31, 2026. (Lexi Critchett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the model, counties would first continue funding schools, roads, police and other essential services. After those obligations are met, local communities would return a portion of remaining revenue directly to residents through annual checks, direct deposits, tax credits, utility bill credits or permanent investment funds. The report emphasizes that the dividends would be financed entirely from existing tax revenue, meaning developers wouldn't pay any additional taxes.

The report estimates that a single one-gigawatt AI data center could generate enough tax revenue to provide households in a typical rural county between $4,500 and $8,900 annually in a "data center dividend," depending on how much revenue local governments dedicate to dividends after paying for public services.

The estimate is based on tax collections from Loudoun County, Va., one of the nation's largest data center hubs. Loudoun collected about $685 million in personal property taxes on data center computer equipment in fiscal year 2024. Dividing those collections by the county's data center electrical load produced an estimate of roughly $165 million in annual property tax revenue per gigawatt of AI infrastructure, researchers estimated.

The report cites new policies in West Feliciana Parish, La., where policymakers are attempting to spread new-found wealth. The parish expects a Hut 8 AI campus to generate about $90 million annually, more than tripling its current budget, according to estimates. Earlier this year, Louisiana lawmakers passed Act 434, allowing local officials to provide property tax credits funded by the new revenue, although lawmakers removed an earlier proposal that would have authorized direct cash payments.

If the cash provision had remained, the report estimates households could have received about $5,600 annually if one-quarter of the revenue were distributed, or $11,200 annually if half the revenue were shared with residents after funding government services.

In another example, Alaska has a "Permanent Fund," or state-owned investment account that collects part of Alaska's revenues from oil produced on state land, invests it in stocks, bonds and real estate, and disburses part of the returns to residents as an annual dividend.

Volunteers hand out yard signs against a data center complex in Canaan Valley on June 30, 2025, after a public meeting organized by the state Department of Environmental Protection regarding an air quality permit application for a gas-fired power plant near Davis, W.Va. (Ulysse Bellier/AFP via Getty Images)
The report outlines several options communities could adopt.

Cash payments. Residents could receive annual dividend checks or direct deposits similar to the payments from Alaska's "Permanent Fund."Property tax credits. Local governments could reduce residents' property tax bills using data center revenue, similar to Louisiana's approach.Utility bill credits. Counties could apply the money directly to electricity bills, benefiting both homeowners and renters while addressing concerns that data centers increase electricity costs. The report notes that a $4,500 dividend would cover the average American household's electric bill for more than two years.Education funds. Communities could place the money into scholarship endowments guaranteeing college tuition for local graduates.Permanent investment funds. Counties could invest the tax revenue and distribute only investment earnings, creating an enduring source of local wealth similar to Alaska's Permanent Fund even if the data center eventually closes.
Cash payments. Residents could receive annual dividend checks or direct deposits similar to the payments from Alaska's "Permanent Fund."
Property tax credits. Local governments could reduce residents' property tax bills using data center revenue, similar to Louisiana's approach.

Utility bill credits. Counties could apply the money directly to electricity bills, benefiting both homeowners and renters while addressing concerns that data centers increase electricity costs. The report notes that a $4,500 dividend would cover the average American household's electric bill for more than two years.
Education funds. Communities could place the money into scholarship endowments guaranteeing college tuition for local graduates.

Permanent investment funds. Counties could invest the tax revenue and distribute only investment earnings, creating an enduring source of local wealth similar to Alaska's Permanent Fund even if the data center eventually closes.

Lyman argues that direct payments create stronger public support than simply lowering taxes or expanding government spending because residents would see the benefit. "I think a lot that opposition is born from the fact that many Americans feel left out of the AI boom. They feel like this economic revolution is taking place without them," said Lyman, noting, "What data center dividends do... is they give every American in rural America a share in the material prosperity that is taking place with artificial intelligence."

The report notes that rural counties possess two scarce assets essential for AI development – land and abundant power – and argues those communities should share directly in the economic gains generated by the AI buildout.
