title: Fmr Biden ambassador blames Trump for Canada playing 'footsie' with China
summary: Former U.S. Ambassador David L. Cohen says Canada is playing "footsie" with China on trade as Trump's hardline policies push allies toward new deals.
story: Former President Donald Trump's U.S. Ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen says there will be "books written" on the trade fallout between allies and weighs in on Canada's bitter opposition to President Donald Trump.
Former U.S. Ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen is blaming the Trump administration's hardline trade pressure for pushing Ottawa into engaging with China.

"I think Canada has tentatively tried to play some footsie with China that the Trump administration may not be happy with," Cohen, who served as President Joe Biden’s ambassador to Canada from 2021 to 2025, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"There is a discomfort with that," Cohen says, while arguing that it is ultimately Canada's reflex to sentiment against President Donald Trump – particularly his hardline trade policies and rhetoric about the neighbor to the north being a "51st state."
VANCE SAYS CANADA FRIENDLIER TO CHINA ON TRADE THAN TO US: 'INSANITY'
U.S. Ambassador David Cohen during the U.S.-Canada Summit in Toronto, Ontario, on April 4, 2023. (Cole Burston/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"One of downsides of the aggressive Trump administration treatment of Canada and many other allies and partners is that the irony is that those policies are pushing those countries to at least consider broader and larger deals with China, which of course is wholly inconsistent with a major thrust of President Trump's international trade policy," Cohen continued. "So, how that shakes out, it's all a matter of degree and balance.

"But I think there's no doubt that the aggressiveness of the Trump administration positions has caused many countries to at least reevaluate whether there are additional deals that can be made with China."

The comments come as U.S.-Canada trade tensions spiral after negotiations collapsed last month. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday accused Washington of seeking dependence rather than partnership.

"The most fundamental issue is that the cumulative U.S. demands revealed that they wanted us to become even more reliant on them, not less," Carney said. "In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership."
TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney might be gaining political cachet in his country over standing up to President Donald Trump, but it is ultimately making tough trade talks more difficult, if not leading Canada into China's hands, according to former Ambassador David L. Cohen. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Notably, the fallout comes just weeks before Chinese dictator Xi Jinping makes an historic trip to the White House to talk trade – something that never happened during the Biden administration despite Biden's onetime quip before the COVID-19 pandemic that "China's not bad folks."
Vice President JD Vance, speaking in Maine last month, accused Canada of giving Chinese goods better treatment than products from American northern border states.
"They treat Chinese goods more fairly than they do the goods that come from the people of Maine: It’s insanity," Vance said. "And what we’ve said to Canada is, ‘Stop it.’"

Cohen, however, was careful not to cast Canada as blameless in the trade feud. He admitted U.S. dairy farmers have legitimate complaints about Canada’s tariff-rate quota system, saying the issue has frustrated administrations of both parties for years.
WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA

"This is one of the totally legitimate trade issues that exists between the United States and Canada," Cohen said. "There is contention there that is hurting American dairy farmers. Yes, I will be honest and clear about that."
"That tension existed under Joe Biden. Was he able to solve that problem? No," he added. "It was something that was discussed and discussed more than once. We just never got there."

Cohen, supportive of Trump's "substance" on trade talks but not the "style," did credit Trump for replacing NAFTA with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, calling USMCA a "terrific deal" that improved continental trade.
TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has the respect of  former Ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen for being a skilled "negotiator." (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)
"I gave President Trump a lot of credit for that because it was a much better deal than NAFTA," Cohen said. "I think he deserves credit for that."
"I do push back at times on some of the rhetoric that President Trump has chosen to use, not necessarily the substance, but maybe the style that he sometimes uses to pursue his substance," he added.

"There are such fundamental differences on the substance of President Trump’s trade policy that I think the treatment of President Trump is different than the treatment of President Biden," Cohen observed. "But when professional negotiators were in the room, they seemed to have been making a lot of progress."

Cohen believes the two sides need to return to professional negotiators, arguing that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Canadian officials had shown they could discuss difficult issues before the talks broke down.
TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE

"I have an enormous amount of respect for U.S. Trade Representative Greer," Cohen said. "He is the ultimate professional trade negotiator, which is why he’s in that job. He didn’t get there by accident. President Trump put him in that job."
By contrast, Cohen said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – who was on the call that Friday night in August when talks broke down at the 11th hour – needs to stay in his lane.

"Secretary of Commerce Lutnick, with all due respect, is not a professional negotiator," Cohen said. "That’s not the Commerce secretary’s job. It’s USTR’s job to negotiate trade deals with other countries."

Lutnick has suggested in interviews about the infamous breakdown in talks that Canadians' politics are at play in keeping Carney from cutting a deal with Trump, a man the provincial leaders and Canadian public have long been disenchanted with.
TRUMP TRADE CHIEF REVEALS WHAT PRECEDED CANADA WALKING AWAY FROM 'BEST DEAL IN THE WORLD'

"Friday at 4 o'clock, the Canadians call: They start adding crazy ideas to the mix," Lutnick said recently. "So, I said to one of the ministers, 'Are you actually trying to blow this up?' And his answer to me was, 'I'm not allowed to say that.' And they blew it up for political reasons only."
Cohen said of Lutnick's account that "until proven otherwise, I take every senior government official at his word, period," and that he has "no way of knowing whether that is true or not."

But, he admitted, Carney taking the nearly finished trade deal back to the provinces did not go over well – particularly amid his rising popularity among Canadians for being an anti-Trump force – because "the premiers of the provinces have more sway in federal policy than most governors do in federal policy."
CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is not in the position as a "negotiator," according to former Ambassador David L. Cohen. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo)

"It appears that Canada made the decision that the deal that was being offered was not a deal that they could accept," Cohen said. "He may have made a judgment that although he and his team had pushed this deal as far as they could, and that it was, in his eyes, as good a deal as he was going to get at that point, that he could not sell that politically in Canada."
"That’s not the same as saying that he was walking away for political reasons," Cohen added. "It’s just the nature of a big, complex negotiation."
TRUMP'S CANADA TARIFF FIGHT REACHES CRITICAL POINT AS HOUSE GOP SUMMONS TRADE CHIEF

Vice President Kamala Harris swears in David L. Cohen as the new U.S. ambassador to Canada at the White House in Washington, D.C., as his wife, Rhonda Cohen, holds the Bible, on Nov. 30, 2021. (AFP via Getty Images)
Ultimately, Cohen said the breakdown between the closest allies and trade partners in the world will be a story long told.

"There are going to be books written about what caused the negotiations to fall apart," he said. "But independent of all the dialogue about that: There is no dispute that these professional negotiators were able to have a civil relationship and talk about really different difficult substantive issues out of the eyes and the ears of the press and with full respect for each other and for the countries. That's my vision for the way in which trade negotiations should occur and they did occur – and it was a two-way street."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Eventually, after the trade-war barbs and tariffs fly and the dust settles, the "professional negotiators" will get things done, Cohen predicted.
"You can’t make a deal if you’re not talking to each other," Cohen said. "Of that, I am 100% certain."

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: $54M CodePink-linked foundation shut down in California pops up at ramshackle Miami home
summary: Arc of Justice, led by CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, lost its California registration and resurfaced as a Florida nonprofit at a Miami duplex.
story: The Miami home listed as the address for a newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit. The same property has also appeared on federal tax filings for the original California foundation. (Credit: AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)
A far-left foundation that bankrolled CodePink and recently reported $54.6 million in assets before being shut down by California regulators has resurfaced at a ramshackle Miami home.

Arc of Justice, led by CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin, lost its charitable registration after years of failing to file required financial paperwork with California. But what appears to be the same nonprofit is now registered at a small, single-story house owned by Benjamin's longtime partner and fellow activist, Tighe Barry, documents viewed by Fox News Digital show.
The sequence of events raises questions about why it fell out of compliance in California.
HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM

The Miami property listed as the address of the newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit features a weathered painted fence and sits behind dense tropical vegetation. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)

Arc of Justice has poured millions of dollars into left-wing and progressive activist organizations over the years, including CodePink, Global Exchange, the Alliance for Global Justice and the National Iranian American Council, according to IRS filings. Federal tax returns provided to Fox News Digital by Arc of Justice's attorney show the California foundation's assets grew from $51.4 million at the end of 2023 to $54.6 million at the end of 2024, while it continued distributing millions of dollars in grants.

CodePink has campaigned against U.S. policy toward China and Cuba and has been accused by congressional investigators of promoting Chinese Communist Party interests — allegations the group has denied.

Benjamin, who has been a political activist for decades and has often disrupted congressional hearings, co-founded CodePink with Jodie Evans, the wife of Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose funding network has come under congressional and federal scrutiny over alleged foreign influence and the use of tax-exempt organizations.
Now it’s Arc of Justice’s finances that are coming under the microscope.

"It's pretty unusual. Most private foundations are fairly scrupulous on their compliance efforts," Patrick Sternal, a former IRS official who specialized in tax-exempt organizations, told Fox News Digital. "So it's unusual for a private foundation with that much in the bank to fall out of compliance and to be suspended."

Medea Benjamin, who led the California-based Arc of Justice foundation and co-founded CodePink, holds a "Let Gaza Live" sign as she is removed by U.S. Capitol Police after interrupting a House Armed Services Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on April 30, 2024. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Registration revoked in California

The California Attorney General's Office, led by Democrat Rob Bonta, revoked Arc of Justice's charitable registration in January 2025 after it failed to submit required annual filings with the state for 2020 through 2024. The foundation had already been suspended for more than a year before the revocation. The state Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital that Arc of Justice had continually failed to respond to the registry's delinquency and suspension notices before its registration was revoked.

Under the revocation, Arc of Justice had 30 days to provide the state with an accounting of its charitable assets and was barred from distributing or spending them without the attorney general's prior written approval.

The years of noncompliance culminated in another notice from California regulators on June 19, 2026, reiterating the outstanding asset-accounting requirement and warning that Arc of Justice couldn’t distribute or spend charitable assets without the attorney general's written approval.

The notice said Arc of Justice would also have to provide regulators with enough information to assure the state that there had been "no loss of charitable assets" if it sought to have its registration reinstated. The Network Contagion Research Institute previously detailed Arc of Justice's regulatory problems in a May report examining the foundation's finances and activities.
FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS
David Levitt, an attorney representing Arc of Justice, said the foundation has submitted filings seeking reinstatement with California regulators.

The Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital on Sept. 3, 2026, that it had not received the required accounting of Arc's charitable assets. At the time, Arc was listed as "REVOKED" and "PAST DUE." As of Sept. 9, its registration remained "REVOKED," while its reporting status had changed to "IN REVIEW."
California's reinstatement rules require a revoked charity to explain why it failed to comply with reporting requirements and respond to Registry notices.
Laurie Styron, CEO and executive director of nonprofit watchdog CharityWatch, said Arc's substantial assets made the compliance failures difficult to explain.
"A foundation with tens of millions of dollars in charitable assets certainly has the resources to comply with basic reporting requirements," she said.

Fox News Digital asked Levitt to provide documentation of the reinstatement filings and to explain specifically why Arc of Justice failed to make the required California filings in the first place. He had not responded to those questions by publication time.
New nonprofit surfaces in Florida
California's latest compliance notice to Arc of Justice came just six weeks after a new Arc of Justice surfaced in Florida.
On May 8, Barry and other people associated with the original foundation incorporated a new nonprofit bearing the same name in the Little River neighborhood in North Miami.
The timing raised obvious questions: Was the California foundation moving to Florida after its charitable registration was revoked, and what was happening to its assets?

The Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital it had not received notice from Arc of Justice of any planned transfer, merger or dissolution and had not approved any transfer of the foundation's assets.
The Miami property listed as the address of the newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit sits at a corner in Miami's Little River neighborhood. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)

Levitt told Fox News Digital that the Florida corporation was created as a "placeholder" while Arc considered relocating its operations from California, but the move was never completed. He said the California corporation was never formally wound down, no assets were transferred and the Florida entity "holds no assets and has conducted no business."

"Arc of Justice, the California nonprofit corporation, currently still holds the assets," Levitt said, adding that they remain professionally managed "in the same accounts they have been in for years."
Levitt subsequently provided Fox News Digital with financial documentation that independently verified that the California foundation continues to hold the assets.
The Miami address wasn't new. The original Arc of Justice had been using Barry's property on its federal tax filings since at least 2017, even as it remained incorporated in California.
Federal filing questions
Questions have also emerged about the original foundation's federal filings.

Arc of Justice's Forms 990-PF for 2023 and 2024 were not publicly available in the IRS database when Fox News Digital searched for them. Levitt subsequently provided Fox News Digital with copies of both returns.

According to Levitt, Arc of Justice's accountant said both returns had been paper-filed and electronically filed, although Fox News Digital has not independently verified when the IRS received or accepted them.
Benjamin was adamant in a phone interview with Fox News Digital that Arc of Justice had filed its returns every year.
"I'm 100% positive. We have filed the 990s every single year," Benjamin said. She also told Fox News Digital she would make sure the missing returns were provided, which they subsequently were.
Benjamin was less certain about the foundation's California regulatory problems, saying she had moved to Florida and that "the lawyer knows more than I do."
CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin in Washington, D.C., on May 11, 2026, with her partner Tighe Barry. (LG for Fox News Digital)

After reviewing the newly produced returns, Sternal said the documents showed Arc of Justice's accountant had at least made an effort to file them, but said questions remained over whether and when they were actually submitted.
"Maybe they are trying to get back into compliance with the IRS," Sternal said. "They still have a lot of clean up to do with California."

Styron similarly said determining when the returns were actually filed was critical to assessing Arc of Justice's compliance. She noted that IRS and state databases can lag behind submissions but said delays of several years would be unusual.
"It would be tough to say more without knowing when forms were signed and filed," Styron said.
While the new records accounted for the foundation's assets and provided the previously unavailable returns, questions remained over when the federal returns were actually filed.

Styron also said Arc of Justice's explanation for creating the Florida nonprofit did not absolve the California foundation's board of its responsibility to file the active organization's required forms on time.

Meanwhile, Sternal, who is now a nonprofit tax attorney at law firm Holtzman Vogel who advises nonprofit and tax-exempt organizations, said there is nothing wrong or unusual about forming a nonprofit in another state. What raises questions, he said, is whether the new Florida organization is intended to take over the original foundation or its assets — a move that would trigger additional legal requirements.
"It's not so easy," Sternal said. "It can be done, it's possible, but there are a lot of hoops that they have to jump through."

Because Arc of Justice remained a California corporation, Sternal said it would have to work with California's attorney general before transferring funds to another organization or moving the foundation out of state.
A painted pig holds a "ONE LOVE" sign on the weathered fence outside the Miami property listed as the address of the newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)
Same name, new home

Along with the new Florida corporation bearing the same Arc of Justice name and Miami address used by the embattled California foundation, two of its three officers also held positions with the original organization.
Maya Danaher, Benjamin's daughter and former treasurer of the original Arc of Justice, is president of the new Florida corporation.
Jonathan Raggett, who served as secretary of the original foundation, is now its treasurer.
Benjamin served as president of the original California foundation but is not listed as an officer of the new Florida corporation.

Meanwhile, Benjamin's longtime partner, Barry, was not listed as an officer of the original foundation but serves as secretary of the new organization. He is also listed as incorporating Arc of Justice in Florida and serves as its registered agent.
Its stated goal is blunt: "WE ARE HERE TO SUPPORT SOCIAL JUSTICE NON PROFITS," according to the articles of incorporation.
All three officers list the Miami house as their address — a 1,334-square-foot Miami duplex owned by Barry, property records show.
The Miami property listed as the address of the newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit, with its street number painted on the front fence. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)
When Fox News Digital visited last month, the small, turquoise-blue, single-story house sat partially obscured by thick palms and tropical plants behind a weathered, multicolored wooden fence.

Fading artwork of colorful cats, pigs, flowers, hearts and peace symbols covered the fence, including a pink pig holding a "ONE LOVE" sign. A large "PEACE" poster hung on the house, while a turquoise-shaded canopy stretched across the property.
Two campaign signs for Democrat Kendrick Meek Jr., who unsuccessfully ran in the Democratic primary election for Florida's 24th Congressional District, stood outside.
Google Street View images from 2022 show the property in brighter colors before the paint faded and vegetation obscured parts of the fence.

The images also show a small white van with its front bumper missing parked outside, with "CODEPINK" written across its side in pink marker along with the Spanish words "Cuba vive y trabaja" — "Cuba lives and works."
The van was not visible when Fox News Digital visited.
The house's number was painted vertically on the weathered front gate — the same address listed by the original California foundation and the newly incorporated Florida Arc of Justice.
A large "PEACE" poster hangs on the turquoise exterior of the Miami property listed as the address of the newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)
SUBPOENAED PRO-CHINA OUTLET DEFENDS ITSELF ON DEMOCRACY NOW!, WHICH PAID SINGHAM-FOUNDED COMPANY MILLIONS
Where did the money come from?
Arc of Justice was formerly known as The Benjamin Fund, Inc., with California corporate records showing the foundation formally changed its name in November 2019.
Its fortune was built largely on Benjamin family money.

Benjamin's father, Alvin Benjamin, was a prominent Long Island real estate developer who founded The Benjamin Companies in the early 1960s. The Benjamin Fund's initial 2003 IRS return shows he contributed a partnership interest valued at $683,715 to the foundation, with Medea Susan Benjamin serving as president.

Much larger contributions followed. In 2010, the estate of Benjamin's mother, Rose Benjamin, contributed $10,863,060, according to the foundation's IRS filing. Five years later, the Estate of Alvin Benjamin contributed another $15 million, followed by another $8,603,450 in 2019.
The foundation's wealth also grew through its investments. In 2020, Arc of Justice reported $12,344,501 in unrealized gains on securities, helping push its year-end assets to nearly $40 million.
Medea Benjamin — identified as Susan Benjamin on the filing — personally contributed $1 million to Arc of Justice in 2022, listing the Miami house as her address.

On June 4, 2024, CodePink's Medea Benjamin interrupts a Capitol Hill news conference in Washington, D.C., organized to commemorate the anniversary of the 1989 Tienanmen Square Massacre and to discuss the "ongoing struggle for human rights and democracy in China." Her sign says, "China is not our enemy." (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The foundation subsequently became a vehicle for funding activist organizations, including Global Exchange, the advocacy group Benjamin co-founded with her then-husband, Kevin Danaher. The organization remains active today, with Danaher still serving on its board, according to its 2024 Form 990.
Benjamin later co-founded CodePink in 2002 with Evans and has remained one of the anti-war group's most prominent activists and public faces.
Arc of Justice would go on to pour substantial sums into CodePink, including $251,500 in 2020 and $355,350 in 2022, according to the foundation's IRS filings.
The newly obtained returns show that Arc of Justice gave CodePink $277,580 in 2023 and another $350,000 in 2024.

CodePink has itself come under federal scrutiny. Benjamin traveled to Cuba in March with fellow CodePink co-founder Evans and far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as part of a roughly 170-person convoy to the communist-run island.

Benjamin later confirmed that the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control, which enforces U.S. sanctions against Cuba, sent CodePink a detailed inquiry seeking information about the trip's financing, logistics, participants and activities.

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin dances barefoot with CodePink activist Tighe Barry at the wedding of Jodie Evans and Neville Roy Singham in February 2017 in Ocho Rios, Jamaica. (Osbourne Chin / Chinphotographic)
Benjamin said the group brought about $600,000 worth of humanitarian aid to Cuba and described the Treasury inquiry as "serious," while also calling it an "intimidation tactic."
Evans and a network of nonprofits funded by her husband, Singham, have also come under congressional and federal scrutiny.

Singham, an American tech entrepreneur who sold his software company ThoughtWorks for an estimated $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai, has directed at least $278 million into six core nonprofits that Fox News Digital previously reported promote socialist, communist and pro-China causes as part of a broader international network of media organizations, activist groups and think tanks.
CodePink is one of those nonprofits.

The congressional investigation remains ongoing, while Singham is separately under federal criminal investigation. Neither Singham nor CodePink has been charged with wrongdoing in connection with the investigations described here.
Medea Benjamin, co-founder of CodePink, holds a sign supporting Cuba at Miami International Airport on March 20, 2026, before a delegation travels to Cuba. (Eva Marie Uzcategui/AFP)
Same name, separate entity
Florida officials confirmed the new Arc of Justice was created as a Florida nonprofit on May 8, 2026, rather than simply registering the existing California corporation in the state.
"That entity is on our records as a Domestic Nonprofit corporation. It is a Florida entity," Florida Department of State regulatory specialist LaCori Brown told Fox News Digital.

The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services separately told Fox News Digital that the new Arc of Justice isn’t currently registered to solicit charitable contributions in the state and has not applied for a charitable solicitation registration or exemption.

The department also said it hasn’t received any filings identifying assets transferred from the California Arc of Justice to the new Florida corporation nor any complaints, referrals or regulatory inquiries concerning the new organization.

Sternal stressed that the available records don’t establish that Arc of Justice's assets were misappropriated or improperly used. He said the foundation's years of California noncompliance remained highly unusual.
"This organization with this large endowment has simply fallen off the radar, as it were, with its filings, with its compliance with California," Sternal said.
"Those don't belong to the officers and directors of the foundation. Those belong to the foundation," Sternal said. "They must be used for public charitable purposes."

Levitt said Arc of Justice's board is still considering moving the foundation out of California and potentially establishing two separate charitable vehicles so the foundation's founder and its officers and directors can pursue separate charitable activities.
For now, the original Arc of Justice remains a California corporation and continues to hold its assets, while the future of the newly incorporated Florida organization remains unsettled.
Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.

title: Armed man accused of lunging at Ohio Dem candidate avoids felonies as prosecutor reveals key evidence
summary: Patrick Havas' own video is the only footage of the Canfield Fair incident after Amy Acton's camp allegedly asked people to stop recording it.
story: Police arrested an armed suspect for lunging at Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton during the Canfield Fair. Acton released a campaign statement praising law enforcement for their swift action, and Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy condemns the violence. Fox News' Alex Hogan reports the latest.
The man who allegedly stormed toward Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton at a recent fair will not face felony charges, the county prosecutor leading the case told reporters Tuesday.
The only video investigators currently have of the incident was recorded by the suspect, Patrick Havas, leaving authorities with little video evidence, Mahoning County Prosecutor Lynn Maro said.
"The information we've received is that the Acton camp requested individuals stop recording shortly before this incident occurred," Maro told reporters on Tuesday.
"So, at this point, the only video we have is the defendant’s. And what's that showing certainly doesn't support filing felony charges."
PISTOL-PACKING MAN KNOCKS OVER FAIRGOERS FORCING HIS WAY TOWARD OHIO GOVERNOR CANDIDATE AMY ACTON, POLICE SAY

Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health and Democratic gubernatorial candidate, meets with local residents while campaigning at Bottoms Up Coffee in Columbus, Ohio, on Monday, April 6, 2026. (Stephen Zenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Patrick Havas was intercepted by Ohio Highway Patrol officers after allegedly knocking over multiple fairgoers as he ran toward Acton at a tent at the Canfield Fair while armed with a Taser and two firearms.

He was initially booked on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct, all misdemeanors. An inducing panic charge was added Tuesday at his arraignment, bringing the total to four misdemeanor counts. Havas pleaded not guilty.

Campaigns have often prohibited or advised against filming candidates to prevent "trackers," or opposition research individuals with cameras, from filming the interactions to look for a politically weak spot to focus on. Then-candidate Bernie Moreno employed audio-jamming technology in 2024, with his campaign acknowledging such to Business Insider. The campaign told the outlet the jammer was only used against trackers and not voters.
When asked by an NPR reporter about online conjecture that the Acton team "overblew" the incident, DeWine reportedly replied the idea is "total garbage.
"No one overblew it. Facts are facts. These are not good situations, and they’re anti-democratic," DeWine said, according to the report.
Maro said the tape showed Havas "walking into the tent" where Acton was, and "calling out her name" before executive protection unit officers from Ohio Highway Patrol interrupted him.
"Then, his phone is either dropped or tossed, and that’s all we have," Maro said.
RAMASWAMY TORCHES DEM RIVAL OVER 'OUTRAGEOUS' COVID-19 CLAIM: 'SPEWING LIES'
"There's never any close contact with the governor, never gets near her — sorry, ‘candidate for governor’," she added.
Fox News Digital reached out to Maro for comment and to obtain a copy of the video in question. An official who picked up the phone at her office said Maro was out but would be checking messages.
A reporter for the NBC affiliate tweeted that their network had also attempted to obtain the video but that officials said they would not be releasing it as part of their "active investigation."
Fox News Digital also reached out to the Acton campaign for additional comment, as well as details around the reported request that people stop filming Acton just before the encounter.

"While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people. Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured," Acton campaign communications director Addie Bullock said in a separate statement.
"This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another."
An Ohio judge ordered Havas to not speak to the press, according to Youngstown’s NBC affiliate, and Havas has been placed under a $5,000 bond and forced to surrender any weaponry in his possession.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Dr. Amy Acton, Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee, marches in a parade. (Jeff Swensen/Getty Images)

Havas is a local to that region of Ohio. He was arrested in 2008 on petty theft and disorderly conduct charges, according to Newsweek. The theft charge was later dismissed after he pleaded no contest to disorderly conduct. He was accused of stealing several movies from a supermarket, including the James Bond film "Casino Royale."

Acton faces Republican entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy in November, as Gov. Mike DeWine is term-limited. DeWine’s lieutenant, former Ohio State Football coach Jim Tressel, declined to run for the office.
Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Reporter’s Notebook: 9/11 is just a history chapter for a new generation of Americans
summary: A quarter century after 9/11, one-third of Americans alive that day are gone, and the memories of Sept. 11, 2001, grow increasingly faded.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Eric Shawn reports from the 9/11 Memorial in New York City on how schools are teaching the history of September 11 to students born years after the attacks. Elementary school counselor Scott Bruce and National 9/11 Memorial and Museum CEO Beth Hillman discuss the importance of preserving the memory for a new generation.
It’s faded.
Not from decay. Not from neglect. It’s simply the passage of time.
The memories are vague. Elusive. Distant. And some who lived it are simply no longer here.
Roughly one-third of all Americans who were alive on 9/11 aren’t around anymore to observe the 25th anniversary of that abominable day. And so the recollections of Sept. 11, 2001, are diluted.
NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS
A boy points toward the center of the reflecting pool at the National September 11 Memorial Museum in New York, on Sept. 11, 2022. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
To some, Sept. 11 is just another day. But it’s something different for those who weren’t around to live and breathe the horror.
To many, 9/11 is like Pearl Harbor Day. Lots of people know about it. They understand it’s what triggered the U.S.’s entry into World War II. But they can’t quite explain much more.

The same with other historical-shifting moments. Aug. 6 and 9, 1945 — the days the U.S. bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, effectively ending World War II. Nov. 22, 1963 — the day a gunman mowed down President John F. Kennedy Jr. in Dallas.
A lot of people remember the Space Shuttle Challenger exploding. But few could tell you that it happened on Jan. 28, 1986.

The quintessence of 9/11 is the date. Kind of like July 4th. A bit like Jan. 6 and the Capitol riot. However, we were told on Sept. 11, 2001, that things would never be the same. But how can those who didn’t experience it understand what "the same" was like if they never lived it?
Just last month, a relative of mine who soon turns 26 asked, "What it was like to fly before 9/11?"

I can regale you with stories about myself and a rag-tag group of high school friends, driving to the Cincinnati airport, clearing security and just wandering around the Delta gates, "hanging out" back in the mid-1980s.
No ticket. No questions asked. Just a visit to Cinnabon.
But the "before times" question about 9/11 is a broader conversation. It’s not just about "what changed" when you take off your shoes and bustle through security to fly.
LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11
American Airlines airplane taking off at Dallas-Fort Worth Airport in Texas. (Getty Images)
A nine-and-a-half-foot-tall plaque hangs in the East Front vestibule of the U.S. Capitol near the Rotunda. It commemorates Flight 93, which crashed near Shanksville, Pa., on 9/11.

It took a few years, but the U.S. intelligence services finally determined that the fourth plane was bound for the U.S. Capitol. That’s where Todd Beamer and a cadre of everyday Americans voted (mind you, at 35,000 feet) to commandeer a drinks cart and rush the cockpit in an effort to seize control of the plane.
"Let’s roll!" Beamer was overheard saying on a cellphone as they charged down the aisle. That two-word phrase became a battle cry for a nation as it waged the war on terrorism.
The Boeing 757 hurtled toward Washington at 563 mph. It was 20 minutes out from the federal city when the plane crashed, upside down, in the Pennsylvania countryside.

Shanksville is now one of those places forever notched into American history. A place not as famous, say, as Gettysburg or Jamestown, but not a footnote, either. Shanksville is part of the vernacular like Shiloh, Seneca Falls, Kent.
People might know that something historic happened there. But they aren’t exactly sure what.

Scores of markers dot the U.S. Capitol, denoting important things from yesteryear. Wander into Statuary Hall in the Capitol and you’ll find the desk locations of eight presidents who served in the House. But the spot where President Franklin Pierce once sat just seems like an historical annotation. Pierce toiled there nearly two centuries ago. And he’s hardly prominent among American chief executives.

There’s a plaque just outside the Old Supreme Court chamber. It tells the story of how Samuel B. Morse sent the first electronic message from that room to Baltimore over a wire in 1844. "What hath God wrought!" reads the plaque, commemorating Morse’s transmission. That event christened the age of near-instant communication – now ubiquitous in the form of news alerts and TikTok videos appearing instantly in the palms of our hands.
But that plaque in the Capitol’s East Front vestibule doesn’t memorialize something that happened there. It marks something that didn’t happen there.
The plaque reads that the actions of the 40 passengers and crew "not only saved countless lives, but may have saved the U.S. Capitol from destruction."
In other words, this global citadel to democracy with its ivory dome might not pierce the Washington skyline were it not for a plane that crashed 167 miles away.
Shanksville. Shiloh. Seneca Falls. Kent.
TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

Donald Trump walks along the Wall of Names of the victims after a wreath-laying during the 23rd anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks at the Flight 93 National Memorial on Sept. 11, 2024 in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. (Jeff Swensen/Getty Images)

I’ve driven the Pennsylvania Turnpike past Somerset for decades now. That’s where the signs direct you north 10 miles to the Flight 93 National Memorial. I budgeted time into my travels to visit the memorial on one frigid, windy morning a few Februarys ago. Inside, you stand at a vista, staring downhill into a small ravine and tree line where the plane crashed.
On that morning, I couldn’t help but notice there was no wildlife to be seen or heard. No deer. No birds chirping.
A disturbing silence.
Perhaps it was the billowing wind of that frosty morning. Maybe the snow. But I noticed no footprints gouging the crisp snowpack.

It was almost as though the animals were aware of something. Dare I say understood what happened in this field a quarter-century ago. Perhaps the local fauna stayed hushed out of reverence for those who perished. A tribute to their heroism, saving the U.S. Capitol.
Or perhaps it was something else.

Maybe the creatures were so reserved because of the malevolence which was also on board Flight 93. One can only speculate that the animals remain hushed because of the peculiar unease enveloping the place. Even on a crisp but blustery winter morning.

Shanksville is a burial ground. And in a few more decades or even a hundred years, those who visit there will walk the paths or peer out over the panorama, trying to grasp the scope of what unfolded there on 9/11.
FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE
Flowers are displayed at the Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial on Sept. 11, 2025, in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. (Jeff Swensen/Getty Images)

You can visit Gettysburg and Antietam and do that now. But much is left to the imagination. Perhaps embroidered by what was picked up in a history class. Augmented by a marker or description on a bronze plaque.

In another quarter-century, there will be even fewer people around who remember 9/11. Another 25 after that and many of those still living might be infirm. Confined to wheelchairs. The final generation of messengers who can speak firsthand about what happened that day. Kind of like when honor flights descend on Washington to visit the World War II Memorial on the National Mall.
It’s just the passage of time.

The plaque inside the Capitol will continue to tell the story. And in many ways, just the fact that the Capitol remains standing tells the story, too. Its presence attests to the bravery that manifested itself somewhere over eastern Ohio and is interred in a western Pennsylvania clearing.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
We know this now. Even though some of what we recall is faded.
But the memories and understanding of the significance will naturally calcify. Details will grow hazy. People will know the date 9/11. But it may just be that — a date. Like Pearl Harbor Day.
President Franklin Delano Roosevelt referred to Dec. 7, 1941, as "a date which will live infamy."
9/11 will live in infamy. But it’s unclear how that date will live in the minds of Americans.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Obama judge's peculiar Trump rebuke ignites fury over 'unprofessional' language: 'Embarrassment'
summary: Three Obama-appointed judges blocked the IRS from sharing taxpayer addresses with ICE on Tuesday, with one calling the argument "weak sauce."
story: A federal judge blocks New York state regulations attempting to force federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to wear identification, marking a significant legal victory for the agency. Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on the ruling, which halts state-level efforts to unmask federal officers. The decision comes as federal sources report ICE made over 51,000 arrests in July.

Critics took aim Tuesday at a federal appeals court after a judge dismissed the IRS’ argument in an ICE data-sharing case as "weak sauce," drawing immediate backlash over the unusual language in the ruling.

"That argument is ‘weak sauce’ where the district court has permitted the IRS to file any necessary notifications ‘under seal,’ thereby shielding any criminal investigative activity from disclosure," wrote D.C. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama in 2013.
"Weak sauce" is slang for something that falls flat and lacks substance.

The lawsuit centers on whether the IRS violated federal tax-confidentiality law by sharing tens of thousands of taxpayer addresses with ICE after receiving requests for information on more than 1 million suspected illegal immigrants. The case was heard by a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel composed entirely of Obama appointees: Pillard, Patricia Millett and Robert Wilkins.
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORCHES TRUMP ADMIN IN LATEST COURTROOM SHOWDOWN, REFERS ATTORNEY FOR BAR REVIEW

President Barack Obama speaks to the press about his nomination of Robert L. Wilkins, a federal district judge, Patricia Ann Millett, an appellate lawyer, and Cornelia Pillard, a law professor, in the Rose Garden of the White House on June 4, 2013. (Ken Cedeno/Corbis via Getty Images)
Critics were quick to slam Pillard’s "weak sauce" comment, calling it an "embarrassment" while others slammed the ruling.

"DHS strongly disagrees with this ruling. We will continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal, and this ruling in no way prevents us from doing so," DHS told Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

"It's an embarrassment to the Court that 2 judges would not have told the author to change a different phrase with the same meaning. Now that is going to be quoted/cited in future cases and it will look sophomoric and unserious," said conservative attorney William Shipley on X.
"Three anti-Trump Obama judges abuse power to impair basic immigration law enforcement. We have a judicial integrity crisis in the federal courts," wrote Judicial Watch president Tom Fitton.
"Why would anyone put that language in a professional document of any kind? That goes beyond legal decorum. It’s just unprofessional across the board," said one user on X.
"I’m all for using accessible language, but the insertion of popular slang in judicial opinions is getting out of hand," another posted to X.
"Make legal writing formal again," wrote D.C. attorney Joshua Prince.
GOP SENATOR UNVEILS BOASBERG ACT TO STOP 'ROGUE' JUDGES FROM HANDPICKING TRUMP CASES
ICE agents depart the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building on Feb. 4, 2026, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (John Moore/Getty Images)
"Did Ketanji write that or some TikTok fan girl? Borderline illiteracy," said one user.
The plaintiffs—including the Center for Taxpayer Rights, Main Street Alliance and two labor unions—argued the IRS failed to ensure ICE’s requests met strict legal requirements.
APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS
President Donald Trump speaks during a Mexican Border Defense Medal presentation in the Oval Office at the White House, Dec. 15, 2025. (Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein)

The judges upheld a lower-court order blocking the IRS from using its current process to provide taxpayer information to ICE, finding that the procedure failed to comply with federal tax-confidentiality law. The judges found that ICE often submitted "either incomplete or insufficiently populated" information, yet the IRS still provided tens of thousands of taxpayer addresses.

The ruling comes as President Donald Trump has made immigration enforcement a central priority, directing the administration to expand border security, detention and deportations while ICE ramps up arrests nationwide.

title: Trump hails 'really big night' for populists in German election after historic victory
summary: Trump celebrated AfD's Saxony-Anhalt election surge on Truth Social, calling the populist party's gains a rejection of Germany's immigration policies.
story: Leaders of the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party celebrates the party's victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state elections on Sunday, in which the party captured 39 seats in the state's 83-seat parliament. Credit: The Associated Press.
President Donald Trump heralded the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's electoral success in regional elections on Sunday in a Tuesday night post on Truth Social.
"Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night," Trump wrote in the post.

"They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!! President DJT," his post concluded.
The German state of Saxony-Anhalt held elections Sunday, and AfD outperformed expectations that predicted the party would secure 40-41% of the vote, according to The Guardian.
AfD surpassed that, garnering 43.8% of the vote while securing 39 seats in the state's 83-member parliament, according to results from the state's election authority.
NEW GERMANY SEX-CRIME FIGURES REIGNITE MIGRATION FIGHT AS EXPLOITATION PROBE EXPANDS

Ulrich Siegmund, center, lead candidate and co-chair of the AfD state parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, celebrates with Alice Weidel, federal chairwoman and co-chair of the AfD parliamentary group in the Bundestag, and Tino Chrupalla, federal chairman and co-chair of the AfD parliamentary group in the Bundestag, after the first results at an election party of the "Alternative for Germany" (AfD) after the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Magdeburg, Eastern Germany, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/dpa via AP)
It's a marked improvement from the young party's last result in the state, as AfD secured only 20% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt's 2021 elections.
'SEND THEM BACK' CHANTS ROCK EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AFTER LANDSLIDE VOTE TO SPEED UP DEPORTATIONS

The anti-immigration party benefited in particular from the Christian Democratic Union of Germany's (CDU) losses, as Saxony-Anhalt's previous governing party dropped 25 seats, ending the election with only 15 seats in the state's parliament, per the results from the election authority.
AfD's parliamentary co-chair in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, credited his party's victory to Germany's unpopular Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a member of the CDU party.
EU ADMITS IT ‘DIDN’T HAVE CONTROL’ ON MIGRATION AS BLOC RUSHES CRACKDOWN AHEAD OF NEW RULES
"Things cannot carry on like this," Siegmund told state broadcaster ARD, adding that "a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz."

German Chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) Party leader Friedrich Merz, left, and Saxony-Anhalt State Governor and top candidate Sven Schulze give a press statement after visiting UPM Biochemicals in Leuna, Germany, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader)
Merz's CDU, like other parties in Germany, refuses to work with AfD, whose Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified as an "extremist group" by Germany's internal intelligence service.
DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING

AfD has been met with complete opposition in Germany, with most parties putting up what leaders and German media have come to categorize as a "firewall" against working with them. The CDU and three other parties that won seats in Saxony-Anhalt's Sunday elections – the Left Party, the Social Democrats, and the Greens – have already publicly stated they will not form a coalition with AfD in the state.

Without an absolute majority, it's unclear how AfD would be able to rule without the cooperation of another party. The party's best hope of forming a ruling coalition would be with the only other party that won seats in Sunday's election, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which took five parliamentary seats.
GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS

Supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) political party gather at the final AfD campaign rally ahead of tomorrow's Thuringia state elections on Aug. 31, 2024, in Erfurt, Germany. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

The state's incumbent governor, Sven Schulze, a member of the CDU, congratulated AfD for its victory, and said, "We as the CDU will also have to deal with this result." But his party's national general secretary, Franziska Hoppermann, remained defiant.

"AfD is a right-wing extremist party. It wants to leave the euro; that would be economic downfall... it works closely together with Russia, it wants a completely different social model," she said, according to The Associated Press. "We will not work with them."
PRESIDENT ALEKSANDAR VUČIĆ: EUROPE VILIFIES TRUMP, BUT WE IN SERBIA SEE A FRIEND

AfD's defacto leader, Alice Weidel, meanwhile, celebrated the result as "sensational," adding that the party’s "hand is outstretched to all who want to make Saxony-Anhalt better and move Germany forward."
Fox News Digital contacted the AfD and the CDU for further comment.

title: Supreme Court chief justice praises outgoing Smithsonian leader who was under pressure from Trump admin
summary: John Roberts praised Lonnie Bunch's Smithsonian leadership as the secretary retired amid mounting Trump administration pressure over museum exhibits.
story: The head of the Smithsonian Institution announced his retirement Tuesday, stepping down amid an escalating clash with the Trump administration over the leadership and direction of the nation’s museums.
Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts praised the outgoing head of the Smithsonian Institution on Tuesday after the official came under fire from President Donald Trump's administration.

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, 73, announced plans to retire this week after more than a year of tension with the White House over how U.S. history is presented at his institution. The Trump administration released a July report earlier this summer laying out its criticisms of the National Museum of American History in particular.

Roberts, who serves as the chancellor of the Smithsonian, hailed Bunch on his departure, saying he "pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story" and that the Smithsonian had "benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership."
FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution Lonnie Bunch listens during an event at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on February 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. First lady Melania Trump donated her second inaugural dress to the museum, which was designed by fashion designer Herve Pierre, who also designed her first inauguration dress. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Prior to his departure, Bunch had pushed back internally on criticism from the White House. The July report argued that the Smithsonian had become "subject to institutional capture by a radical, activist ideology that is fundamentally opposed to telling the noble, honest story of the great country we know and love."

Bunch responded with an internal email to staff members, acknowledging that there is "room for improvement," but arguing the report was "not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History."
TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig appears with former first lady Jill Biden and Smithsonian Institution Secretary Lonnie Bunch during the presentation of Biden's 2021 inaugural dresses at the Smithsonian on Jan. 25, 2023. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP)

"At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America's story. As public servants and the keepers of this institution, we are charged with helping a nation find understanding, hope and clarity and as part of that duty, we are dedicated to excellence, reflection and growth," he wrote.

Bunch appears to have relented to pressure after the latest move by the White House, which saw Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and White House Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley warn that the Smithsonian could lose access to artifacts and grants from the federal government if it continues with its current leadership.
SMITHSONIAN'S TAXPAYER FUNDS FACE CHOPPING BLOCK AS GOP DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY FOR 'WOKE' HISTORY
The Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History is seen from the Washington Monument on June 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
Burgum and Haley wrote a letter to Congress last week laying out concerns about ideological capture and potential misconduct among the Smithsonian's leadership.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The administration has recently uncovered evidence that the Smithsonian leadership's institutional culture may have resulted in significant violations of Federal antidiscrimination law, including creating a hostile work environment and engaging in practices that classify individuals and allocate opportunities, funding and other benefits on the basis of race, ethnicity and other protected characteristics," the letter read.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: George Bush welcomes top officials to his home state for 9/11 remembrance on 25th anniversary of attacks
summary: George W. Bush and Condoleezza Rice will share their reflections on 9/11's legacy at a Dallas event ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
story: The 9/11 Memorial & Museum observes the 25th remembrance of the 2001 terrorist attacks, aligning with America's upcoming 250th anniversary. President Elizabeth Hillman discusses the critical need to educate nearly 100 million Americans born after 9/11 on the event's historical significance and the national response.

DALLAS — George W. Bush was president during the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks, and he is marking the 25th anniversary of the day that changed America forever by hosting a solemn remembrance event in his home state.

The event, called "A Legacy of Service: America at the 25th Anniversary of 9/11," will take place at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas, and kicks off at 6:30 p.m. local time on Wednesday evening.

It will feature a conversation between former President Bush and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who "will share their reflections on the legacy and meaning of 9/11—how the day changed the country, how it continues to shape American life, and how the call to serve remains as urgent as ever," according to the webpage for the event.
George W. Bush speaking to cadets at the Virginia Military Institution in 2002. (Photo by PAUL J. RICHARDS/AFP via Getty Images)
9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

A moderated discussion between General Dan Caine, the current chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and former Deputy National Security Advisor J.D. Crouch, who served in that role under Bush from 2005 to 2007, is also part of the program.

Melissa Stockwell, a two-time Paralympic triathlete and Army veteran who was awarded a Purple Heart and Bronze Star after losing her leg in Iraq, is a featured guest. So is Jared Lyons, a Navy veteran and CEO of Student Veterans of America.
MASSIVE WORLD TRADE CENTER STEEL BEAM ARRIVES AT WEST POINT, UNITING 9/11 HEROES WITH GENERATION SENT TO WAR
Smoke pours from the twin towers of the World Trade Center after they were hit by two hijacked airliners in a terrorist attack September 11, 2001, in New York City. (Robert Giroux/Getty Images)

"Together, these conversations will offer a thoughtful, elevated reflection on a defining moment in American history and on the enduring commitment to service that continues to strengthen the nation," the webpage for the event says.

As part of the 25th anniversary commemoration, Bush painted 16 works of art that "reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and resilience that emerged from one of the most defining moments in American history," that will be displayed at Freedom Hall at the Bush Museum through September.
Bush was known for his painting hobby when he occupied the White House and in the years after he left office.

President George W. Bush threw the ceremonial first pitch before Game 3 of the World Series between the New York Yankees and Arizona Diamondbacks at Yankee Stadium on Oct. 30, 2001, in the Bronx, New York. The Yankees defeated the Diamondbacks 2-1. (Rich Pilling/MLB via Getty Images)
The Bush Presidential Center has also invited the public to join in a moment of remembrance on Friday morning, alongside local first responders.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Bush was president on Sept. 11, 2001, and was visiting an elementary school for an education event when he was informed that America was under attack. He first used the phrase "war on terrorism" on Sept. 16, 2001, and officially declared a campaign during a Sept. 20, 2001 joint address to Congress, which kicked off the 20-year war on terror.
He was elected for a second term in 2004 and retired to Texas with his wife Laura, and the two have maintained a relatively low profile.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Socialist politicians are 'more racist than the KKK,' says Black Dem official urging voters to ditch El-Sayed
summary: Karen Whitsett slams Abdul El-Sayed and Democratic Party leaders she says take Black voters for granted, calling out his ties to Hasan Piker.
story: Michigan's 2026 Senate race heats up as progressive nominee Abdul El-Sayed faces intense criticism over his policy platform. Florida Representative Kat Cammack rails against El-Sayed's socialist agenda, comparing his campaign tactics to a used car salesman. Cammack warns that these progressive policies will ultimately drain the wallets of working-class families while offering nothing but empty promises in return.

An elected Democratic official in Michigan is rallying her community against U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and claims those within the socialist rise of her party take Black voters for granted.

"It doesn't change, it's just different slave owners," Democratic Michigan state Rep. Karen Whitsett told Fox News Digital in reference to Democratic Party leaders who believe Black voters are a monolith who should only support left-wing candidates.
She claimed that El-Sayed is not working in the best interest of Black Michiganders and that the far-left wing of her party is "more racist than the KKK."
JASMINE CROCKETT WARNS DEMOCRATS ARE TOO FOCUSED ON WHITE VOTERS, IGNORING BLACK VOTERS

Rep. Karen Whitsett, D-Mich., speaks during a meeting with patients who recovered from COVID-19 in the Cabinet Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on April 14, 2020. President Donald Trump's plan to reopen the economy was unveiled as part of the administration's coronavirus response. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

Whitsett called out prominent Black voices known for rallying the community's vote for Democrats — specifically naming Al Sharpton and controversial Detroit pastor Horace Sheffield III, an El-Sayed campaign surrogate. She accused the pair of working to "keep the knee on [Black voters'] neck."
Whitsett said Black voters are "waking up" and are "realizing the power of our vote."

"You can see the serious divide of the crazy socialist far-left and especially the White women," Whitsett said. "They are the worst and the most racist that there possibly ever could be. They're, I think, they're more racist than the KKK."

"Are you trying to help the Black community or are you trying to kill it?" she rhetorically asked. "Are you trying to keep people stupid and ill-informed or what? Because right now I can't tell, right? Is this voter education or are you just trying to make sure you count your slaves on the plantation."
MICHIGAN GOP LAWMAKER CASTS DOUBT ON EL-SAYED’S SOCIALIST DENIAL AS POLICIES TELL ANOTHER STORY: ‘SHARP ODDS’
El-Sayed's values aren't aligned with hers, Whitsett said, adding that she doesn't think he has the best interest of Black voters at heart, either.

"I'm going to stand on Bible first, and I'm going to stand on community first," she said. I don't care about moving up within the Democratic Party. I don't care about making sure my pockets are better."
El-Sayed's campaign did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment on Whitsett's criticism of the candidate and the Democratic Party's leftward shift.
Whitsett is not running for re-election and will retire when her term expires at the end of the year.
Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, at a campaign event in Detroit, Michigan on August 2, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

"I always try to be a voice of reason, and I'm not a go along, get along. So, my whole thing is it has to make sense, and I am definitely family over party. God over party is of the utmost importance," she said.

"So for me, when you point that out to people, it's just common sense that to people, that's just common sense that El-Sayed is not the candidate," she continued. "There's just no way. It doesn't line up. It doesn't line up Biblically, and it doesn't line up with common sense."

Noting that she does believe everyone should have medical insurance, Whitsett harped on El-Sayed's campaign promise of Medicare for All. She said the progressive candidate hasn't adequately explained how that system will be implemented, and what it means for Americans when they visit the doctor.
EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER

"This Medicare for All, it's not for all. It's not going to change the dynamics of how many doctors there are, or nurses or blood draws or anything else. You're now going to put the government in your health system, and they're going to decide for you."

Hasan Piker, left, listens as Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks in a green room before a campaign rally, Tuesday, April 7, 2026, at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Mich. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

El-Sayed already finds himself in hot water for palling around on the campaign trail with socialist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets and is known for making antisemitic comments.
El-Sayed has refused to condemn Piker, instead painting him as a "streamer from California" who has no bearing on the race in Michigan, despite inviting Piker to Michigan to campaign for him.

Many Jewish Democrats in Michigan have vowed not to support the far-left candidate, saying in an open letter they feel "threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed, which has included demonization of Jews, equivocation on terrorism, exclusion of Jewish Americans from public life, and expression of implacable hatred of the world’s only Jewish nation."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Record gas prices squeeze Americans as summer travel season ends, midterms loom and Iran war wages on
summary: Gas prices hit a record $4.15 per gallon over Labor Day weekend, shattering the previous high and posing a significant political test for Trump.
story: Senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reports on the Trump administration’s economic policy wins and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s outlook for gas prices returning to around $3 a gallon on 'The Story.'

As the summer travel season came to a close, Americans faced the most expensive Labor Day at the pump on record, extending the squeeze on household budgets for millions who hit the road over the holiday weekend.
AAA estimated that nearly 40 million Americans would drive over the holiday, paying unprecedented prices for gasoline.

The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.15 per gallon on Tuesday, up about 5 cents from the previous week and nearly 96 cents higher than a year earlier. The price shattered the previous Labor Day record of $3.82, set in 2012, and marked the first time the national average topped $4 during the holiday weekend.
FORGET GASOLINE: THIS OVERLOOKED FUEL COULD RAISE THE PRICE OF NEARLY EVERYTHING YOU BUY
Drivers fill up at a gas station as fuel prices remain elevated following the Labor Day weekend. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The spike came despite a seasonal trend that typically brings some relief after Labor Day, when summer travel winds down and gasoline demand eases. This year, however, elevated crude oil prices tied to the Iran conflict offset that typical decline.

Fighting in the Middle East raised concerns about disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that carries roughly one-fifth of the world's crude oil. Those concerns kept crude oil prices near $90 a barrel, limiting the seasonal decline in gas prices motorists typically see after Labor Day.

The record prices pose a political challenge for President Donald Trump, who campaigned on affordability and pledged to bring gasoline below $2 per gallon. His push to expand domestic oil and gas production has made energy costs a key test of his economic agenda, particularly as the Iran conflict drives crude prices higher.
With Americans still facing elevated everyday costs, record Labor Day gas prices could contribute to making affordability a major issue heading into the midterm elections in November.
TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER
While the national average reached $4.14 per gallon, prices varied significantly by state.

America's west was hit hardest. California had the nation's highest average gas prices at $5.78 per gallon, followed by Washington at $5.47, Hawaii at $5.41, Oregon at $4.98, Alaska at $4.96, Nevada at $4.91, Idaho at $4.62, Arizona at $4.52, Utah at $4.42 and Montana at $4.38.

At the other end of the spectrum, Indiana had the nation's cheapest gas at $3.44 per gallon. It was followed by Texas at $3.69, Oklahoma and Mississippi at $3.71, Louisiana at $3.75, Arkansas at $3.77, South Carolina and Kansas at $3.78, Alabama at $3.79 and Wisconsin at $3.80.
TRUMP JUST BROKERED A DEAL WITH THE COUNTRY SITTING ATOP THE WORLD’S LARGEST OIL RESERVES
President Donald Trump has made lowering energy costs and improving affordability central promises of his economic agenda. (SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images)

With the summer driving season now over, drivers would typically expect prices to decline as fuel demand eases. But any relief at the pump will depend largely on whether crude oil prices retreat from recent highs or remain elevated by continued tensions in the Middle East.
